title: Surface Laptop Ultra review: a different kind of MacBook Pro
snippet: This MacBook Pro lookalike is designed for developers. After setting up Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra, I spent five minutes just staring at it. I wasn't surprised by its MacBook Pro-like design or blown away by its bright display. I was trying to work out what I'd actually do with a $5,900 laptop. This isn't just any regular Windows laptop. Microsoft has teamed up with Nvidia to build a high-end laptop to showcase Nvidia's new Arm-based RTX Spark chips. It's a big moment for Windows on Arm, as these chips can run demanding AI models locally, alongside the latest AAA games and creative apps. The promise is compelling, but the reality of local AI is much messier. Getting the most out of the S … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
After setting up Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra, I spent five minutes just staring at it. I wasn’t surprised by its MacBook Pro-like design or blown away by its bright display. I was trying to work out what I’d actually do with a $5,900 laptop.

This isn’t just any regular Windows laptop. Microsoft has teamed up with Nvidia to build a high-end laptop to showcase Nvidia’s new Arm-based RTX Spark chips. It’s a big moment for Windows on Arm, as these chips can run demanding AI models locally, alongside the latest AAA games and creative apps. The promise is compelling, but the reality of local AI is much messier.

Getting the most out of the Surface Laptop Ultra, especially my top-of-the-line model, requires coding experience or the patience to experiment with models and AI agents until you find something that works. If that sounds like you, Microsoft might have built the Windows laptop you’ve been waiting for. If not, this might not be the MacBook Pro competitor Microsoft was hoping for.

6

Verge Score

$2599

The Good

Beautiful hardware design

Magnetic USB-C charging

Large haptic trackpad

The Bad

Local AI feels like a beta

Some bugs with sound and display

CPU performance is underwhelming

It feels like Microsoft has finally built the hardware to rival Apple’s pro laptops, thanks to an all-aluminum design, large haptic trackpad, and high-end finish. Even the “nightfall” color is just like Apple’s space black.

There are plenty of meaningful differences, though. The 15-inch MicroLED display can run at up to 2,000 nits of peak HDR brightness, at 262 pixels per inch (3270 x 2180); the MacBook Pro peaks at 1,600 nits. That makes it the brightest display Microsoft has ever shipped on a Surface Laptop. Unlike the MacBook Pro, it’s also a 3:2 touchscreen, perfect for writing code, reading text, or editing photos.

The port selection is similar to the MacBook Pro, with one very big change. You get three USB-C ports, a USB-A port, a single HDMI 2.1b port, SD card reader, and headphone jack. Where it really differs is Microsoft’s new Magnetic Connect. It works just like the old Surface Connect, but through the USB-C port on the right-hand side. Just bring the connector close to the port, and it snaps into place. When you’re not charging, that port works just like the rest of the USB-C ports on the laptop.

Magnetic Connect is one of my favorite additions on the Surface Laptop Ultra. I love how you can reverse the magnetic USB-C charging end, attach it to the power brick, and use the regular USB-C connector at the opposite end of the cable to charge the rest of your devices.

Left-side ports: HDMI, 2x USB-C, and a headphone jack.

Right-side ports: SD card reader, USB-A, USB-C.

The haptic feedback on the large trackpad is also a welcome addition. It works with things like clicks, drags, and window alignment throughout Windows 11, and the tactile feedback triggers in apps like PowerPoint as you drag and align objects or images in a deck, too. It’s subtle enough to make it feel like you’re really moving windows or interfaces around, but I do wish more apps supported it.

Microsoft has included a 1080p front-facing camera above the screen. The quality is fine for video calls, and it supports Windows Hello face authentication and Windows Studio Effects like automatic framing, eye contact, and background blur.

Not all of the Surface Laptop Ultra hardware is impressive, though. I’ve had issues where I’ve unplugged the charger at 100 percent only for Windows to then immediately report 97 percent battery life. Plugging in would put it back to 100 percent and then it would immediately drop back to 97 percent again each time I unplugged.

The magnetic USB-C charger is an impressive addition.

It seemed weird so I asked Microsoft about the behavior, and it’s designed this way to make a battery last longer. “When it’s plugged in and the battery is full, the device pauses charging rather than constantly topping off, and resumes only once the level drops to 95 percent,” says Microsoft spokesperson Moses Nsereko. “This reduces wear over time. While plugged in, the indicator shows 100 percent to indicate a full charge. When you unplug, it shows the battery’s exact level right away, which may be a few percent lower.”

I’ve run into some issues with the display, too, where either things felt slightly laggy or there was noticeable ghosting. Moving a window around rapidly sometimes left a little trail. Changing power settings from the default “best power efficiency” mode to “best performance” seemed to fix most of the laggy feeling, and the backlight ghosting seems to be less noticeable the longer you run the laptop.

I also heard some loud pops and bangs from the built-in speakers on the Surface Laptop Ultra. They were loud enough to sound like firecrackers, and I thought the battery was about to die before I realized it was just speaker interference. Rebooting the Surface Laptop Ultra solved this one, but it’s happened a couple of times now.

Speaking of rebooting, I’ve noticed that rebooting the Surface Laptop Ultra is surprisingly slow. This seems like something Microsoft could easily fix with an update, though.

The Surface Laptop Ultra can run complex local AI models.

Local AI models and agents

The RTX Spark that powers the Surface Laptop Ultra is designed with local AI models and agents in mind. The variant I’ve been testing has a 20-core CPU that was codesigned by Nvidia and MediaTek paired with a 6,144-CUDA-core GPU — roughly comparable to a mobile RTX 5060 — plus 128GB of unified memory and a 1TB Gen 5 SSD. It’s the top-of-the-line model at $5,899, and I think if you’re considering this particular laptop spec then you have a very specific use case in mind. The base version is $2,599, and it comes with an 18-core CPU, 5,120-CUDA -core GPU, and 24GB of unified memory.

Out of the box, Microsoft prompts Laptop Ultra owners to pick an AI agent. You can choose between Hermes, OpenClaw, and Perplexity. I tried out Hermes and OpenClaw over the past week, but I ran into issues getting OpenClaw to work initially. A reinstall fixed a gateway issue, and then I could name my agent and start using it for local AI tasks.

I configured both Hermes and OpenClaw to use the Qwen3.8-27B model, one of the more powerful local AI models. Because it uses the full power of the Surface Laptop Ultra, it will spin up its fans at full throttle and 100 percent GPU for even the most basic of queries. I asked Hermes to resize and convert some photos from PNG to JPG, a task that would take seconds using a PowerToy utility. It took minutes to complete, all while the fans were buzzing away and the laptop was getting hot.

It’s probably my fault for using such a large model for a basic task, but without testing every single local AI model it’s hard to know which one to pick for each task you need. I asked OpenClaw to build me a smart home dashboard, but it spent 30 minutes spinning up the laptop’s fans and calling various tools to eventually produce nothing but an error.

I don’t have a base Surface Laptop Ultra to test, but it’s easy to see that 24GB of unified memory will mean fewer local AI models to choose from.

Local AI models are best for coding tasks right now.

I struggled to come up with many compelling use cases for the power of these chips for local AI work. A lot of tasks could simply be done far more quickly and without the laptop fans spinning up by using a free cloud model. The power here is really in leaving the agent running at full throttle to build something overnight, or run a task across large datasets that would normally cost a lot of money in cloud tokens.

I did like that I could do things locally, though, without worrying about the privacy aspects of cloud models. I fed Hermes some audio and video files and it went ahead and created a local llama.cpp server to enable audio transcription. It took some fiddling to get it working, but it could certainly save me having to install transcription apps or pay for a cloud service like Otter.

The thing I didn’t like is that these agents are far from user-friendly, and I’m surprised that Microsoft or Nvidia hasn’t developed its own local AI interface that simplifies a lot of this work. I need to spend more time with both Hermes and OpenClaw, but as someone who doesn’t code it’s clear this is all really targeted toward developers and power users.

Gaming and creative tasks

The Surface Laptop Ultra might not be an official gaming laptop, but it’s certainly capable of running far more of the latest games than Apple’s MacBook Pro. Normally I’d be nervous about Windows on Arm and gaming, given the weak GPU on the Qualcomm Snapdragon X series chips. But this is the first time we’ve seen an Arm CPU paired with a stronger Nvidia GPU, and most games run well for a laptop that’s not the size of a gaming one.

Instead of running a bunch of benchmarks at different settings, I decided to try and find the optimal settings that would allow me to play at around 60fps or more in each game. Because this is an RTX GPU, you also get full support for DLSS, Frame Generation, and ray tracing. So you can enable Frame Generation if you want to get to 120fps to match the 120Hz display.

I was able to run Black Myth: Wukong at 70fps on average at native resolution (3270 x 2180) with medium settings and DLSS performance mode enabled. I ran the same medium settings and DLSS performance in Cyberpunk 2077 and averaged 66fps, and Forza Horizon 6 managed an average of 57fps.

Most games will need to run at medium settings and DLSS performance or balanced to get around 60fps, but there are some exceptions where you’ll need to lower settings or resolution. Gears of War: E-Day averaged 40fps on medium settings and DLSS performance, and I only managed to bump this to 48fps on low settings. I also had to move Doom: The Dark Ages to low settings and DLSS performance to hit an average of 60fps.

Gears of War: E-Day running on the Surface Laptop Ultra.

I’m spoiled by using an RTX 5090 on a 32-inch 4K screen every day with maxed-out game settings, but I didn’t mind the look of medium settings on a 15-inch display. It felt more like dropping down to console settings, and in some games it’s hard to distinguish the texture differences on a smaller display. I’m one of those gamers who prefers to run at 60fps with lower settings rather than max out the settings and have to play at 30fps, though.

While game compatibility is good for most titles, there are some where you’re going to run into emulation issues. Horizon Zero Dawn Remastered was limited to 30fps at 1440p regardless of whether I used low or medium settings. I believe this is because the game is CPU-heavy, so a native Arm port would probably help for this type of game.

There aren’t many native Arm games, though. I tried out the new Arm version of Marvel Rivals, and it averaged 64fps with medium settings and DLSS performance and 75fps with low settings. I think we’ll only see Arm ports where there’s a lot of CPU activity involved that the Prism emulator — which translates CPU instructions from x86 to Arm — can’t handle well enough, because otherwise it’s very capable.

We may see more Arm ports for games that have anti-cheat engines. Anti-cheat engines are a lot more complicated to emulate, so developers have to create Arm-compatible versions. While games like Arc Raiders, Counter-Strike 2, Dota 2, and Fortnite all work out of the box, Nvidia and Microsoft are working with EA, Activision, and Riot Games to get titles like Battlefield, Call of Duty, Valorant, and League of Legends fully supported.

The Surface Laptop Ultra is also a very capable machine for creative and everyday tasks. I managed to export our 4K video test in two minutes and 18 seconds on the Surface Laptop Ultra using Premiere Pro. That’s around a minute behind the top-of-the-line MacBook Pro, but beats the base M5 chip and is around 30 seconds behind the M5 Pro. I did have to create this using Premiere Pro’s own export tool, rather than sending it to Media Encoder like how we usually run this test. There seems to be a bug in the beta Arm version of Media Encoder that prevented it from running the export correctly.

Where the Surface Laptop Ultra really falls behind Apple’s M5 chips is in CPU performance. Single-core and multi-threaded CPU tests like Geekbench or Cinebench show how much weaker the MediaTek CPU is against a $6,999-plus MacBook Pro 16 with an M5 Max or even an M6 Mac Mini. Even some of the GPU tests for Geekbench show the RTX Spark falling behind Apple’s MacBook Pro, and the Puget Bench Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and DaVinci Resolve are all noticeably behind the M5 Max.

I’ve also been testing the battery life of the Surface Laptop Ultra, which seems to be around seven hours if you’re using local AI models and a mix of apps and gaming. If you’re doing less intensive work, it’s averaging out at 10 hours or more. I’ll know more the longer I use the Laptop Ultra, so check back for updated battery impressions.

Surface Laptop Ultra is designed for Blender and other creative apps.

The Surface Laptop Ultra doesn’t really offer a clear performance advantage over the MacBook Pro outside of some AI workloads like image generation and the ability to run CUDA compute natively. It’s not transformative for the Windows world like the M1 chips were for macOS, largely because Qualcomm already supercharged Windows on Arm with its Snapdragon X series two years ago. That makes it difficult to recommend unless you’re specifically interested in running local AI models, coding, or experimenting with AI agents.

The Surface Laptop Ultra, and Nvidia’s RTX Spark in general, targets developers and power users who want a laptop that can handle those workloads alongside creative apps and the latest games. For that audience, there’s a lot to like. For everyone else, more affordable laptops can handle everyday productivity, creative work, and some light gaming without the hefty price premium.

Microsoft has come closer than ever to building a Windows alternative to the MacBook Pro. The hardware looks and feels great, and Nvidia’s GPU brings CUDA support and decent gaming capabilities to a high-end laptop design. But the Surface Laptop Ultra’s biggest selling point is also its biggest question mark: local AI. It all feels like a work in progress. If you’re ready to experiment with it, this could be a compelling glimpse of where Windows laptops could go next. If you’re not, it’s a lot of money to spend on an experiment.

title: Google AI Mode and AI Overview updates work to elevate links
snippet: Google is continuing its work to make links more prominent in AI Mode and AI Overviews. more…
fullText:
Google is continuing its work to make links more prominent in AI Mode and AI Overviews.

Moving forward, inline links will appear “higher up in responses more frequently.” Google is also making the links that appear at the end of some AI responses “more engaging and prominent.” The “Dive Deeper” section will feature image thumbnails and have a “more clickable design.”

Elsewhere, prominent carousels for timely articles and Preferred Sources are coming to additional locations and languages around the world after launching earlier this year. Usage of the customization feature has grown 7x since then.

AI Search is testing a new section at the top of AI responses for sites that are the “one or two official places on the web to complete a specific task or get the exact info you need.” Google will also add “context about why each link is useful.”

	

Another test is for “clickable creator and publisher names on video results.” This will take you to Search profiles, which are available for eligible creators and publishers.

These profiles give you a quick way to learn about creators and their broader work, giving you even more context.

title: Google rolling out Universal Cart that lets you shop the web and find deals with Gemini, Search
snippet: Following its announcement at Google I/O earlier this year, Google’s new Universal Cart is now rolling out in the US, giving you the ability to shop the web and watch for deals using Search, Gemini, and more. more…
fullText:
Following its announcement at Google I/O earlier this year, Google’s new Universal Cart is now rolling out in the US, giving you the ability to shop the web and watch for deals using Search, Gemini, and more.

Universal Cart is designed to be an “intelligent” cart that works across more than just a single retailer. Through Google products such as Search and Gemini, you can save products to the cart and also pull in promo codes and monitor for deals for items in the cart.

Google says:

The cart puts you in control, helping to organize your shopping, keep track of items you love from across retailers, stay on top of promos, and enjoy effortless checkout powered by the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP). Today, Universal Cart is rolling out in the U.S. across Google Search and in the Gemini app.

The core pitch here is the ability to add items to the Universal Cart through various touchpoints in Google services. Through Search and AI Mode, you can save shopping items to the cart, or you can do it through the Gemini app and conversations with the AI. Multiple retailers can have products in the cart with Google then linking to those retailers for eventual checkout.

	

While items are in the cart, Google will monitor for deals and price changes, alerting you if the price drops.

Similarly, Universal Cart can find “hidden” deals such as promo codes or even offers on your credit card such as cashback, helping you to change payment methods if there’s a way to score a better deal.

Google says this is powered by Wallet and that it “understands your card perks and can intelligently help you choose between payment methods.”

This is US-only for now, and comes just ahead of the busy holiday shopping season.

title: Opera Air gets a minimalist makeover with a focus on distraction-free browsing
snippet: Opera is relaunching its Opera Air browser today with a redesign that is both conceptual and practical for a more focused browsing experience. Here’s what that means. more…
fullText:
Opera is relaunching its Opera Air browser today with a redesign that is both conceptual and practical for a more focused browsing experience. Here’s what that means.

Opera Air relaunches with renewed focus on distraction-free browsing

In early 2025, Opera announced Opera Air, which the company described as “the first web browser built around the concept of mindfulness.”

Since then, the company has been refining not just Opera Air but the entire family of browsers it offers, including Opera One and Neon.

Today, Opera is relaunching Opera Air with an update that builds on its minimalist design and overall experience, and “keeps distractions to a minimum to give people more room to focus on what matters.”

Here’s Opera:

Air starts simple, with a clean interface and additional tools available when wanted. Messaging and social media apps can also be added to the sidebar.

The redesign also gives Air a new visual look. Refreshed wallpapers use open spaces, perspective, and natural textures, automatically adapting to Light and Dark themes.

Less on the surface doesn’t mean less underneath. Air comes with a built-in ad blocker for faster, less cluttered browsing and a free VPN for added privacy and protection online.

In keeping with the original idea for Opera Air, today’s update still includes Soundscapes, organized into four categories, that combine music and ambient sounds to help users focus or relax.

Ambience brings sounds such as Sea Waves and Spring Forest, while five new Soundscapes feature original music composed specifically for Opera Air. Among them is Hyperfocus, a more energetic track designed for settling into a task and staying there.

And speaking of focus, Opera Air also offers a set of features that help users take a break and regroup before resuming their browsing session.

That includes customizable break reminders that bring up breathing exercises, also divided into four categories (Destress, Refresh, Box Breathing, and Relax), as well as neck stretches.They can also be accessed from the sidebar, alongside Soundscapes.

Opera Air is free and available for macOS and Windows, and you can learn more about it here.

title: Google Messages adding ‘enhanced protection mode’ as Android works to combat phone scam
snippet: For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, Google is announcing new Android features to help combat messaging and phone scams, including enhanced protection mode in Google Messages. more…
fullText:
For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, Google is announcing new Android features to help combat messaging and phone scams, including enhanced protection mode in Google Messages.

Google is introducing an “enhanced protection mode” for its Messages app. Billed as providing the “most powerful and intelligent defenses” against complex scam threats, this mode starts with Scam Detection leveraging Private AI Compute. Google Messages will use “cloud Gemini models to evaluate complex message context and understand a scammer’s intent more quickly when you’re in a conversation with an unknown sender.”

This secure cloud analysis augments and extends our existing on-device detection, allowing us to identify novel and sophisticated attacks, actively uncovering and stopping abusers who try to hide their tracks

Private AI Compute, which is used by Pixel Screenshots and other apps, encrypts data and processes it in a secure space that Google cannot access for any other purpose.

The existing link protections work to flag malicious and phishing websites. With enhanced protection mode, on-device Gemini Nano uses “real-time web signals to evaluate whether an unfamiliar link is trustworthy before you tap.” This feature is available on the Pixel 10+, Samsung Galaxy S26 series, Galaxy Z Flip 8 and Z Fold 8. and “other select devices.”

	

The final feature adds redesigned warnings that “give you extra time and clearer context to pause before tapping links sent from numbers not saved in your contacts.”

This feature was previously only available on devices in select countries or on devices with Android Advanced Protection enabled 

Enhanced protection mode is an opt-in setting that is rolling out over the “coming weeks.”

Meanwhile, Google is expanding on-device Scam Detection for chat notifications beyond Pixel to HONOR, Infinix, iQOO, itel, JOVI, Motorola, OPPO, OnePlus, realme, TECNO, vivo, and Xiaomi devices. 

On the phone scam front, automatic screen-share privacy that hides sensitive info (like passwords and banking information) in native apps will soon apply to Chrome and WebView on Android 15+ devices.

Google will block apps from “quietly enabling call forwarding in the background” to combat one-time passcode theft. This call forwarding protection will be available starting in early December on Pixel and other select devices.

If a scammer attempts to trick you into manually typing an MMI forwarding code on your phone’s dial pad, Android proactively warns you before it can take effect.

title: I’ve Tested Echo Shows and Nest Hubs. Here’s How Apple’s HomeView Display Stacks Up
snippet: Apple’s new HomeView faces steep competition from Amazon and Google’s well-established smart displays. Here’s what I think, based on my past reviews.
fullText:
The HomeView, announced Tuesday and available on Nov. 13, is Apple’s first-ever smart home display and a new way to control smart home devices or interact with Siri AI. But Apple has significant catching-up to do in this space, because its top competitors have been in the game for a while.

I’ve been testing Amazon’s Echo Show smart displays since they first launched in 2017, and started trying out Google Nest Hubs – originally the Google Home Hub – in 2018. Since then, both brands have released multiple smart speaker models, adding and ditching various features. (And sometimes canceling entire lines – anyone remember the Facebook Portal?)

	

			

	

			

									

						Apple HomeView					

							

		

That means the stylish HomeView has a chance to learn from past smart display mistakes and differentiate itself in buyers’ eyes, including the Echo Show 11 and the 10-inch Google Nest Hub Max I use at home. Now that we have details and I’ve tried out the Apple HomeView in person, I have several thoughts for anyone considering which smart display to buy.

			

More from CNET

Nuts and bolts: Apple’s stylish display faces a challenge

Apple

The HomeView looks great. It immediately reminds me of the Echo Show 11, with the screen mounted on a low-set, domed base housing the speakers. With the discontinued Echo Show 10, Amazon tried an auto-rotating base that followed people as they moved, but it frequently bumped into things, which annoyed me. So I’m glad to see this display is stationary.

At 7 inches, the HomeView is also tiny.

CNET Smart Home and Robotics Editor Ajay Kumar, who tested out the HomeView at a press briefing, reported that others at Apple’s event complained that the screen was too small. Based on my experience with smart displays, I wholeheartedly agree: It’s significantly smaller than any competitor models made for the same spaces. I’m confused as to why Apple added a screen better suited to a bedroom smart clock than to a tabletop display.

Those Liquid Retina details and colors look great, and maybe a screen this size was the only way to keep the price below $300. But it also hampers some of the best uses of a smart display, like making video calls and watching movies. Apple may have demonstrated Pluribus playing on the HomeView, but I can guarantee you won’t want to watch it on a 7-inch screen from halfway across the kitchen. You won’t be able to catch many details of those Siri “Start Cooking” instructions or FaceTimes with the family, either.

There’s a reason both Amazon and Google have been steadily inched up the size of their flagship smart displays. They’re useful as second TVs or video guides and they need the screen real estate to pull it off. I know from experience that screens under 8 inches don’t cut it unless you’re about a foot or two away.

The wall-mounted HomeView looks remarkably good.Ajay Kumar/CNET

But wait — there are also wall-mounting options. Google Nest falls way behind here, but you can buy the HomeView as a wall mount version, and Amazon offers a few wall-mounted Echo Shows, too. Kumar said the wall-mounted version of the HomeView looks good, but it also requires professional installation to hide the wired power connection, which will drive your bills well beyond $300. While the result looks amazing, the wired plug-in model may be more practical. Keep in mind that the cheapest wall mount Apple sells with the HomeView costs an additional $60. 

I’m also worried about the size of the display on a wall mount, too. The Echo Show 21 ($500) offers a 21-inch touchscreen for your home, as well as a built-in Fire TV platform for watching shows. That much screen real estate still feels more useful than a 7-inch display, which seems more like a security system and lighting hub than an all-purpose station.

The battle of voice assistant AIs — I still think Amazon’s is better

The HomeView will tap into information from your personal apps.Apple

I’ve pitted the big three voice assistants against each other in the past, and recently tested which can predict the weather best. Gemini for Home is fine, if a little boring, and very accurate. Siri is snappy when controlling Apple Home devices, but falls behind elsewhere. Alexa Plus, however, is my favorite for smart display use.

Alexa Plus is chatty by nature, but also offers several different personalities to choose from, an option other voice assistants don’t have. Amazon’s integration with Echo Shows has numerous benefits, like showing you the previous details of your conversation so you can keep it going more easily, or displaying extra information on request. Alexa AI is overconfident and sometimes insists it can do things it can’t, but this is an issue with many LLM chatbots.

My favorite Alexa Plus ability is integration with third-party apps, an area where other voice assistants haven’t caught up yet. You can use an Echo Show and Alexa Plus to order food from GrubHub or Uber Eats without lifting a finger, or arrange for an Uber ride from across the room. You can also buy tickets on Ticketmaster or make reservations with OpenTable via Alexa, and Amazon continues to add new integrations for me to test.

Alexa Plus now offers compatibility with some very useful apps, both new and returning.

Tyler Lacoma/CNET

There’s no indication that Siri AI includes such third-party app support on the HomeView. Apple says, “HomeView supports compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone,” but doesn’t give many details, and I haven’t seen signs that the HomeView/Siri AI combo will support services or bookings like Alexa Plus can.

But Siri’s AI does win on some accounts, carving out capabilities that Alexa Plus and Gemini for Home don’t have. From the examples Apple showed, it looks like Siri can naturally search your email and texting apps to bring up messages, recipes or other info, something the other voice assistants can’t (Gemini only does this on phones, with the right permissions). You can also customize Siri AI in unique ways, like speeding up or slowing down the voice, which I really like for ease of use and accessibility.

I still prefer Alexa Plus overall, with its chatty asides, personalities to play with and connections to useful third-party apps. I’m looking forward to testing Siri AI on the HomeView to see just what it can do and if Apple adds further integrations. Pricing could also work in Siri AI’s favor, depending on what iCloud Plus subscription is needed to enable all features. If you’re not an Amazon Prime member, Alexa Plus costs a steep $20 a month to fully enable, and Gemini for Home is priced similarly, so Apple could step ahead if Siri AI costs are low.

Smart home controls are where Apple’s ecosystem shines

Just like an Apple Watch: You can customize the look of your HomeView, depending on your preference, from standard clocks to a calendar to a family to Snoopy.Apple

While Kumar explored how the HomeView worked, he noted that he used an Echo Show to control his smart home and said that, “the result is… functional, which is the highest praise I can offer it.”

It’s not an uncommon frustration with the Matter standard and home hubs. Linking multiple smart devices to Alexa or Google hubs and using smart displays for control can be challenging. Interfaces are sometimes wonky, and you can’t always find the settings you want. Devices disappear and need to be reconnected or updated to work again. Voice assistants may not recognize commands that previously worked.

Here, Apple’s tightly knit ecosystem and careful management of the Apple Home app offer a distinct advantage. Kumar saw how the HomeView could effortlessly find and pair with compatible devices, which he compared to setting up a new pair of AirPods. Siri AI can also offer personalization based on facial recognition or manual profile creation, with speedy customization options.

As with HomePods, you can also hand off content between iPhones and the display. Other little Apple tricks, like an instant Find My map displayed to locate missing Apple items, are also included. It already feels more seamless than both the past smart display experiences Kumar and I have had, which is enticing.

The only issue is device support, which tends to be more limited for Apple than other platforms. The company has come a long way in addressing this with its new line of security cameras, a smart lock, and a smart thermostat announced at the Welcome Home event, all clearly made to work with Siri AI and Apple Home. Third-party smart locks also tend to be highly compatible with Apple. Other devices like smart plugs, smart bulbs and third-party security cameras still lag behind, so you may have to look harder to find Apple-friendly models.

Keep in mind that competition also plays a role. Google allows some products, like my Nest cameras and Nest Learning Thermostat 4, to work on Echo Shows with Alexa, but there’s no Apple support. Amazon brands like Ring and Blink will only work with Alexa, not Google or Apple platforms. Choosing the Apple smart home may come with self-imposed limitations.

Always double-check your streaming capabilities

Apple’s streaming support is a huge question mark for the HomeView.Apple

Equipped with two custom full-range drivers, a down-firing woofer and two passive radiators, the HomeView’s audio proved “significantly more impressive than I expected,” according to Kumar, but not quite as good as a full-size HomePod. For reference, the Echo Show 11 has two full-range drivers and a woofer but no passive radiators, and the Nest Hub Max has two 10-watt tweeters and a 30-watt woofer.

All three can fill a standard room with sound, but in my experience, the most important part by far is whether they support the music streamers you use.

Apple Music is a given for the HomeView, but again, Apple is light on integration details and intent on pulling people into all things Apple. While Apple mentioned the new HomePod Mini 2 supports TuneIn Radio, iHeartRadio, and Audacy, it doesn’t mention any specific services for the HomeView, so if you rely on other apps, you may want to check for confirmation. Based on Apple’s past HomePod support, only Deezer and Pandora have been easy to add in addition to the listed services.

Alexa and Google Home’s audio streaming options are extensive.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Meanwhile, my Echo Show supports not only Amazon Music and Apple Music but also Deezer, Spotify, Tidal, Pandora and SiriusXM. Likewise, my Google Nest Hub supports not only YouTube Music, but Apple Music, Deezer, Spotify, Pandora, Amazon Music, TuneIn Radio, and iHeartRadio. As you can see, for maximum music streaming options, you may want to choose a smart display other than the HomeView, or wait to see if other apps add compatibility.

If you don’t mind the small screen, the same caveat applies to video streaming services, but even more so. The HomeView is highly focused on Apple TV, and I don’t know what other streaming apps will be available, if any.

Video options also appear much broader on Echo Shows and Nest Hubs.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Google’s Nest Hubs, meanwhile, can handle a variety of apps through Google Casting, including Netflix, Disney Plus, Hulu, Paramount Plus (I assume Skydance support will be included), Sling, Viki, Starz, Tubi and others. That makes it one of the best smart display choices for watching videos.

My Alexa app is currently a mess and desperately needs redesigning, but through my Echo Show touchscreen, I can access Prime Video, Netflix, Hulu, YouTube, Peacock, TikTok, Disney Plus, HBO Max and many more. Larger Show models gain native support for Fire TV, which enables all kinds of streaming apps, too.

Pricing is comparable, but Apple’s display will still cost the most

Echo’s wall-mounted models are the only options that cost more than the HomeView.Chris Monroe/CNET

Some of Apple’s home prices shocked me. $400 for a floodlight security camera is wild when competitors charge around half as much for similar capabilities. But aside from the small screen, HomeView’s $299 price is in line with other current flagship smart displays. Amazon’s Echo Show 11 starts at $250, but sees discounts around the holidays, something Apple is more averse to. Bumping up to wall-mounted Show 21 brings costs to $500. Google’s Nest Hub Max, while increasingly hard to find these days (I’m hoping Google will release a new Hub soon) is available from around $230 to $250 at various stores.

So while you’ll pay more for a HomeView, it’s not as huge a jump as you see with some other Apple products.

One more thing: Don’t forget about iPads

The iPad is an alternative screen for your home.Sarah Tew / CNET

Of the big three display brands, Apple has by far the most complete support for its tablet computers across the various iPad lines. That introduces an alternative I must bring attention to: You could just use an iPad.

Add a prop cover as a stand, and an iPad could serve many of the same roles as a HomeView on various counters and tables, but with a much larger screen and much more compatibility with apps you already use. Plus, you can pack it away or switch it to other purposes, like serving as a small laptop or a workout companion, when you’re at home.

Two downsides to the iPad approach. First, they cost a lot more, starting around $750 for the iPad Air and $600 for the iPad Mini. Second, unless you’re an AirPods owner or have a HomePod to connect to, sound will always be better on a HomeView.

I’ll provide more details as we get to testing the HomeView and Apple’s other new home products in the coming months, but for now, you should have enough to decide whether you want one for the holidays or are prepared to wait.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home						
					

											

								

											Tyler has worked on, lived with and tested all types of smart home and security technology for over a dozen years, explaining the latest features, privacy tricks and top recommendations.
With degrees in business management, literature and technical writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon, gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. But when not at work, he can be found hiking the trails, trying out a new food recipe for his loved ones, keeping up on his favorite reading or gaming with good friends.

title: Apple reportedly gearing up for strong iPhone 18 sales
snippet: While the iPhone 18 Pro is out, the entry-level model has been held back until early next year. That’s likely because the company wanted to maximize early production capacity and memory availability for the Pro model, alongside the iPhone Duo. But even this far ahead, one leaker has suggested that supply-chain orders indicate Apple is optimistic about demand for the base model … more…
fullText:
While the iPhone 18 Pro is out, the entry-level model has been held back until early next year. That’s likely because the company wanted to maximize early production capacity and memory availability for the Pro model, alongside the iPhone Duo.

But even this far ahead, one leaker has suggested that supply-chain orders indicate Apple is optimistic about demand for the base model …

Apple broke with tradition this year in launching only the Pro models of the new iPhone lineup, that is, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. The base model iPhone 18 was nowhere to be seen.

There are likely a couple of reasons for this. First, the memory shortage meant that the company probably wanted to ensure there was enough supply for both the two iPhone 18 Pro models and the iPhone Duo.

Second with the iPhone Duo a more complex device, production demands are likely greater, even for a model likely to sell in relatively modest numbers thanks to the high price. For that reason, Apple may have wanted to give its manufacturing partners some breathing space by not launching the standard iPhone 18 at the same time.

Apple begins its production runs significantly ahead of iPhone launches in order to build up stock ready to meet initial demand. Production of the iPhone 18 is expected to begin at the end of November.

Leaker Fixed Focus Digital (FFD) says that inventory levels indicate that the company is gearing up for a significant stockpile of devices. This presumably refers to component orders placed within Apple’s supply chain.

The standard version of iPhone 18 is scheduled for production at the end of November, and judging by the inventory levels, the stockpile is quite substantial.

9to5Mac’s Take

Order levels within Apple’s supply chain are not necessarily a reliable indicator of production volumes. Apple prefers to have multiple suppliers for as many components as possible in order to negotiate the best possible pricing as well as protect against any issues experienced by individual manufacturers. It’s possible that FFD has visibility into a single supplier that happens to be favored by Apple at this point in the run-up to production. 

For this reason, we shouldn’t read too much into this report. However, the leaker does have a decent track record, so let’s call it an interesting indication that Apple may be expecting strong demand for the upcoming iPhone 18.

title: Google’s new ‘Shop devices’ tab sells Pixel and Samsung Galaxy devices side by side
snippet: Google has launched a new “Shop devices” portal that lets interested buyers pick up a Samsung Galaxy smartphone from the Google Store, right alongside a Pixel phone or Watch. more…
fullText:
Google has launched a new “Shop devices” portal that lets interested buyers pick up a Samsung Galaxy smartphone from the Google Store, right alongside a Pixel phone or Watch.

The Google Store is the main place you’d go to buy a Pixel smartphone or any other Google product, and that’s all the store directly carries. But, over the past several months, Google has been not-so-quietly selling Samsung devices. Through the Play Store’s Play Points program, buyers have been able to place an order for Samsung Galaxy devices through the Google Store. 

Until now, that’s been the only way to do it. Just through selective offers or redemptions.

Now, Google is elevating this with a dedicated “Shop devices” tab in the Play Store. This addition, which appears to be rolled out fairly widely, pulls up a page with a variety of Google Pixel and Samsung Galaxy devices including:

	

Galaxy S26 and Galaxy S26 Ultra

Pixel 10a

Pixel Watch 4

Pixel 11 Pro Fold

Galaxy Z Flip 8

Google TV Streamer

Pixel 11

Galaxy Watch 9

Pixel 11 Pro

The order is a bit scattershot, but the functionality is simple enough. Pick your device, check out via the Google Store. You’ll get the same 10% Google One cashback benefit as well as the ability to use Google Store credit on Samsung devices and Pixel devices alike. 

Notably, Google hasn’t raised the price of Samsung’s Galaxy S26 series through this portal yet.

title: Our Favorite Air Purifier Brand Just Released a Smaller, More Affordable Option
snippet: Coway unveiled the Airmega Mighty2 Mini today.
fullText:
Coway, the brand that nabbed the top two spots on CNET’s best air purifier list after our recent testing, just released a brand-new, compact unit that’s part of its popular Airmega lineup.

The Airmega Mighty2 Mini features ultra-quiet operation, a multi-stage filtration system and a compact design that’s 40% smaller than its larger counterpart, the Airmega Mighty2. But the price tag may be the biggest draw.

The top two picks on our list, the Airmega 450 and the Airmega 400S, retail for $499 and $680, respectively, while the  Mighty2 retails for $270. Yet the Mighty2 Mini comes in as the most impressive steal at $170. 

		

			

How the Airmega Mighty2 Mini works

I received the Airmega Mighty2 Mini ahead of its launch. Although our lab team in Louisville, Kentucky, hasn’t yet put it through our rigorous air purifier testing, a few things were clear off the bat. To start, this unit is cute. The sleek and compact design makes it ideal for any room, but its quiet operation makes it ideal for bedrooms and nurseries. The Airmega Mighty2 Mini is available in white, beige and green.

It has a manufacturer-listed range of 19.2 to 49 decibels, depending on the mode used. For reference, 49 decibels is comparable to moderate rainfall. When it was set to its lowest speed, I never noticed it was on, but at its highest, I could definitely hear it. However, it was still significantly quieter than my window air-conditioner unit or tower fan.

The Airmega Mighty2 Mini has four modes and three speeds. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNETv

It has eco, turbo, sleep and smart modes, as well as three speeds, a timer option and a washable pre-filter, a carbon filter, and a HEPA filter that can remove 99.97% of particles 0.3 microns or larger. It weighs less than 10 pounds and is easy to move from room to room.

Unlike some other air purifiers, including some from Coway itself, this affordable option lacks app connectivity. Still, it has a simple built-in air quality monitor with a four-color LED indicator at the top of the unit that shows the air quality in your room at any given time.

Our lab tested the larger Airmega Mighty, and during the particle-removal test, it removed 90% of fine particles in 90 seconds with the fan on high and in 2 minutes and 45 seconds with the fan on low. Although these are decent results, other units, including the top two Coway options, outperformed it in particle-removal speed. Still, the prices of the Airmega Mighty options are hard to beat.

One of my favorite things about this unit is how easy it is to remove and replace the filters. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

In our next round of air purifier testing, we will include the new Airmega Mighty2 Mini to see whether it can impress us as much as larger Airmega models.

title: Half of United flights have Starlink Wi-Fi – here’s how to check yours
snippet: United Airlines first introduced Starlink Wi-Fi on its flights starting early in 2025, the airline says nearly half of its flights currently offer the high-speed satellite internet service. It’s now introduced a new way to let you check whether your flight has the service … more…
fullText:
United Airlines first introduced Starlink Wi-Fi on its flights starting early in 2025, the airline says nearly half of its flights currently offer the high-speed satellite internet service. It’s now introduced a new way to let you check whether your flight has the service …

The airline says that it intends to hit 100% Starlink coverage by the end of next year, while current installation rates depend on the fleet. For mainline aircraft flying long distance routes, the current figure is 37%, while United Express regional jets have significantly greater coverage at 68%.

United already has more Starlink-equipped planes than any other airline in the world and is installing it on about 20 aircraft per week with plans to complete installations by the end of 2027. More than 250,000 United customers on average fly on a Starlink-equipped plane every day onboard more than 2,500 flights – nearly half the airline’s daily departures.

Starlink is now active on more than 635 United mainline and United Express aircraft and the airline has already flown more than 37.7 million passengers on Starlink-powered aircraft across more than 538,000 flights, powering 14 million devices.

United already notifies you about the availability of Starlink Wi-Fi in preflight emails and texts, but it’s now introduced a tracker in case of any equipment changes on your route. Airlines do sometimes need to swap aircraft at relatively short notice to account for issues like technical faults and flight cancellations that leave planes incorrectly positioned for their next scheduled flight.

Simply go to this tracking link within two days of your departure, entering your flight number and departure date. If you check further ahead, the tracker will show you the percentage likelihood based on recent flights on the same route, but it’s only within 48 hours that you’ll get a generally reliable answer.

title: YouTube begins rolling out GIF support for comments very slowly; it’s for a reason
snippet: It’s been less than a month since YouTube said it planned to let users post GIFs in the comments section. The time has come, and this is just the beginning of a gradual rollout. more…
fullText:
It’s been less than a month since YouTube said it planned to let users post GIFs in the comments section. The time has come, and this is just the beginning of a gradual rollout.

	

Reddit is being inundated with r/YouTube reports of users seeing GIFs in the comments under videos on the YouTube app. The conversation around the ability to post GIFs under a video is louder than the feature itself. It looks like YouTube is pushing this update in a gradual rollout, since a number of posts online center around not having the feature, but seeing them posted by other users.

YouTube said this would be coming last month, noting that users would be able to post a GIF under videos and Shorts. Any GIF posted will come from a library within the app, according to the company’s announcement. It’s unclear if users will be able to upload their own animated files.

What’s also unknown is how gradual this rollout is. Plenty of users don’t have the option, and it isn’t limited to Premium subscribers, it seems. Fortunately, YouTube is making this available slowly for the time being. Once it gets going, it’s not hard to imagine what a YouTube with a GIF-filled comments section would look like. It’s possible one may never see text in a comment again.

	

YouTube also announced other features when it broke the news about its new GIF comment system. The YouTube app will let users set custom feeds based on quick prompts, and Ask YouTube will get additional features centered around product comparisons. All three features are slated for “this Fall,” so it might not be much longer before YouTube comment sections are filled with GIFs instead of text.

title: Meta launches new Muse Spark Open model, optimized to run on Mac Studio
snippet: Meta today unveiled Muse Spark Open, which it says is the “most capable US open-weight model to date.” For Apple users, Meta says Muse Spark Open is optimized to run on the Mac Studio powered by M5 Ultra. more…
fullText:
Meta today unveiled Muse Spark Open, which it says is the “most capable US open-weight model to date.” For Apple users, Meta says Muse Spark Open is optimized to run on the Mac Studio powered by M5 Ultra.

In a blog post, Meta explains that Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and brings “leading agentic capabilities to your desktop for the first time.”

Today, we’re releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weight model to date. Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal model with 816B total parameters (42B active) and a 1M-token context window. Built for coding and agentic work, it excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning.

Meta’s blog post specifically touts that Muse Spark Open leverages Apple’s latest version of MLX. MLX is an open source array framework created by Apple and optimized for the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon.

Using the latest version of MLX, Meta says that Muse Spark Open was optimized for Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, and that “together they’re the best way to run a powerful model on your own desktop.”

Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra’s integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.

Muse Spark Open is available now through Hugging Face. Apple has also published a new article on its Machine Learning Research website touting how MLX on Mac “lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment.”

Apple and Meta working together is a surprise given the icy history between the two companies. In an interview with Axios, Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said they are “excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again.” Wang explained that Apple and Meta have been working together for several months. Wang credits Daniel Gross, a former Apple executive, with playing a “really big role in kind of getting the two companies to work nicely together.”

title: Hey Google, where is the next Nest Hub?
snippet: Apple’s long-rumored smart home display is finally here and it begs the question – why hasn’t Google released a new Nest Hub in half a decade? more…
fullText:
Apple’s long-rumored smart home display is finally here and it begs the question – why hasn’t Google released a new Nest Hub in half a decade?

Following the explosive popularity of smart speakers, 2018’s Google Home Hub helped usher in a new step forward with smart displays, combining the always-listening hotwords with additional functionality in visual responses, video streaming, live camera feeds, and more. It was a pretty immediate hit that was eventually rebranded as the “Nest Hub” and later spawned two sequels: the larger Nest Hub Max and the second-gen Nest Hub.

And that’s where we’ve been for five years now.

Half a decade later, Google’s smart display efforts have been completely silent. Outside of bringing Gemini for Home to smart displays in the exact same capacity as smart speakers, virtually nothing has changed on a Nest Hub in the past few years. Just look at our coverage over the past couple of years – no new features, no groundbreaking changes of really any kind. Google impressively replaced the underlying operating system without anyone really noticing, but functionally, it’s just status quo.

	

That’s not to say status quo isn’t still good. The Nest Hub experience still checks a lot of boxes. Visual responses to voice commands is at the center, with easy controls for your smart home and doorbell previews also being core to it all. Top that off with casting of video apps (great for the kitchen), setting timers, and the Nest Hub Max’s ability to double as a Nest Cam, and it all gets the job done. There’s a reason that myself and millions of other Nest Hub buyers still use these devices. 

But did Google really hit a wall so hard that not only nothing has changed on the software side, but hardware has just been completely stagnant? Maybe, but it’s hard to believe if so, especially as Amazon has been plugging away with new form factors and ideas for its Echo Show series for years now – the bigger Echo Show 15 with Fire TV is a great example; I’d love a tiny Google TV for parts of my home that can’t justify a “real” TV.

Fast forward to today, and now we’ve got Apple’s entry to the market. “Homeview” is a little 7-inch display on an iMac-like pedestal that also mounts itself to the wall. At its core, there’s not a ton here beyond what you get on a Nest Hub. Visual responses to voice commands are the central functionality, with Apple also picking up Nest Hub Max’s ability to recognize individual users and adjust the software accordingly. Where Apple builds on it is with faster software – Nest Hub, even at launch, has always been a laggy mess – and a reboot of its smart home efforts with other new hardware in tow. It’s really just a ton of Apple’s usual polish to integrations and apps, just in the form factor of a Nest Hub.

But again, it begs the question; where is Google in all of this? 

Google hasn’t ignored the smart home space over the past few years, with its own smart home reboot coming in 2021’s Nest Cam revival and further releases since, as well as a complete reinvention of the Home app to better serve as a hub for not just Google’s ecosystem, but a deep catalog of compatible smart home devices. And there’s been a lot of good on that front, with the more recent effort to use Gemini helping to clean up what was a crumbling experience in Assistant. It’s still not perfect, but Google’s ecosystem has all of the right parts to back up a smart display. 

The last time Google acknowledged smart displays was around when the Google Home Speaker was announced. Roughly a year ago this week, in fact. At the time, Google Home chief Anish Kattukaran called the smart display the “ultimate form factor” for the smart home. And yet, it’s now Apple that’s delivering on that promise before Google.

Google seems to have something in the works, with “Google Home Display” showing up in code earlier this year, but nothing has come of it yet. 9to5Google readers pitched their ideas for the product, including keeping the Pixel Tablet’s detachable display and generally improving the performance and the display quality, the latter being things that Apple’s Homeview display absolutely do.

	

Google’s lack of action is going to hurt it pretty directly here. Apple’s launch isn’t cheap at $300, but for iPhone users, it’s a pretty easy sell. Just like how the Nest Hub was an easy sell as a smart home controller that displayed your pictures, that’s all Apple has to say to sell its own. Amazon’s Echo Show has a bigger uphill battle because, frankly, who wants to invest in Amazon’s ecosystem, but Google at least served as a nice middle ground for everyone. Out-of-the-box integration if you use an Android phone, and just a step or two if you already have a Gmail account, which is true of basically everyone anyway. But, right now, Google simply doesn’t have an option. Not only does it not have a competing option, but it just doesn’t sell anything. 

What do you think?

title: Smartphone shipments dropped by 20%, lowest point in 14 years amid memory crisis
snippet: RAMageddon continues to have wide effects throughout the tech industry, with a new report revealing that the smartphone market has just hit its lowest point in well over a decade. more…
fullText:
RAMageddon continues to have wide effects throughout the tech industry, with a new report revealing that the smartphone market has just hit its lowest point in well over a decade.

Counterpoint Research reports that global smartphone shipments dropped by 20% in Q3 2026, reaching the lowest numbers in the past 14 years. The last time smartphone shipments were this low, Samsung’s latest release was the Galaxy S3. 

Yikes.

The drop has not only impacted overall shipment figures, but also the share of the market that major smartphone brands take up. Chinese brands including Xiaomi, Vivo, and Oppo all make up a smaller share of the overall market in Q3 2026 compared to the same time the prior year, with Samsung continuing to hold the top spot at 23% of the overall market and Apple at 22%, up from 19% and 18%, respectively.

	

Counterpoint says that Samsung’s overall shipments only dropped by 3%, with the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s success playing a major role in the company’s quarter. Meanwhile, a recent report claims that Samsung makes no profit when it sells Galaxy phones at this point.

Apple, meanwhile, saw a 22% year-over-year decline with the absence of its base iPhone 18. Oppo and Vivo both saw drops of around 20% while Xiaomi dropped shipments by 30%.

title: Will HomeView support third-party apps? Here’s what Apple says
snippet: Apple today announced HomeView, a $299 smart home display with a 7-inch screen that lets users control connected accessories, make FaceTime calls, and enjoy music and video content. But what about third-party apps? Here’s what Apple says. more…
fullText:
Apple today announced HomeView, a $299 smart home display with a 7-inch screen that lets users control connected accessories, make FaceTime calls, and enjoy music and video content. But what about third-party apps? Here’s what Apple says.

Apple HomeView’s support for third-party apps will be limited

Apple says the new HomeView smart home display is “designed for life at home,” with a wide range of features for managing connected accessories, staying organized, and enjoying entertainment.

That includes everything from controlling smart home devices and checking calendars to watching videos, listening to music, and making FaceTime calls.

However, one question Apple’s announcement didn’t fully answer is the extent to which HomeView will support third-party apps.

According to Apple, in addition to a selection of Apple apps, including Music, Podcasts, and Safari, HomeView will also support “compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone for a familiar experience across devices.”

Interestingly, the fine print for this feature differs between Apple’s HomeView marketing page and the product’s press release.

While the produt page says:

Subscription may be required to access some content and services. Some applications are not available in all areas.

The press release, however, includes an additional detail (emphasis ours):

Subscription may be required to access some content and services. Some applications are not available in all areas. Select apps require a paired and compatible iPhone nearby.

Some of Apple’s own first-party apps will also be available from the iPhone, the company notes. That includes Audiobooks, Apple Music Classical, News, and TV.

Apple has yet to detail how the iPhone proximity requirement will work, and whether developers of apps in supported categories will need to take any additional steps to support HomeView.

	

According ot Wired, “a handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps.” Wired adds that “if your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup.”

So it looks like HomeView’s third-party app support will rely on the existing CarPlay framework, rather than requiring developers to build apps specifically for the device. It remains unclear, though, whether this will extend to other CarPlay app categories, such as communication and AI assistants, or also be limited to media apps.

We have reached out to Apple for clarification on how third-party app support will work, and will update this post if we hear back.

Next week’s iPhone Duo arrival expected to be first of four weeks of new products

We already know that iPhone Duo will be available next Friday, October 23, HomePod mini 2 on October 30, and HomeView and Apple TV 4K on November 13.

He explains: “Apple retail stores are going to have a big floor reset on the evening of Thursday, November 5 into Friday, November 6.”

Gurman believes the forthcoming touchscreen MacBook Pro redesign, M6 iMac and MacBook Pro, and OLED iPad mini will all be available in stores starting November 6. He reported earlier today that those product unveilings are set for October 28.

Apple would then launch the following products in four successive weeks:

October 23: iPhone Duo

October 30: HomePod mini 2

November 6: New Macs and iPad mini (per Gurman)

title: The ‘renewable’ iPhone Duo display layer may help buyers justify the price
snippet: The iPhone Duo starts at $1999 for the 256GB model and rises to an eye-watering $3199 for the 2TB version – but a “renewable” inner display layer may help buyers to justify spending so much money on a phone. Apple has addressed the biggest problem experienced with folding phones to date via a surprisingly affordable option … more…
fullText:
The iPhone Duo starts at $1999 for the 256GB model and rises to an eye-watering $3199 for the 2TB version – but a “renewable” inner display layer may help buyers to justify spending so much money on a phone.

Apple has addressed the biggest problem experienced with folding phones to date via a surprisingly affordable option … 

One of the biggest problems of Android folding phones has been a crease that is visible when new and that tends to become even more so after repeated folding and unfolding over time. Apple reportedly put a huge amount of work into a hinge and display design intended to minimize this effect, and early hands-on sessions confirm that the crease is barely visible when new.

Despite this, however, it’s still likely that some visible degradation of the inner layer will occur over time. Indeed, the company has acknowledged this, with hardware lead Kate Bergeron saying that the company has worked hard to help it “wear in as long of a manner as we can.”

That’s a potential problem with a device so expensive it’s likely that most buyers will want to hold on to it for far longer than a typical iPhone, but Bergeron also revealed that this inner cover layer is replaceable once the crease does finally become more visible.

It’s actually replaceable, which is a really nice thing for the customer, that you can peel off that layer and get a new one.

We learned at the time that a replacement costs just $19 with AppleCare, and we now know that the price without is $49. For a machine costing $2k and up, that’s a surprisingly affordable way to make the inner display look like new again. Anyone thinking they might justify the price by holding on to the phone for a number of years may very well find this the deciding argument.

What’s your view? Does this renewability make the price of the device more palatable? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Sony just canceled a promised Android 17 update for one of its Xperia phones
snippet: Sony isn’t exactly known for speedy Android OS updates, but the company has now completely canceled an Android 17 update for one of its Xperia phones. more…
fullText:
Sony isn’t exactly known for speedy Android OS updates, but the company has now completely canceled an Android 17 update for one of its Xperia phones.

In a notice on its website, Sony says that it will not provide an Android 17 update to the Xperia 10 VI despite initially promising “three Android OS upgrades” for the device. 

Sony announced the Xperia 10 VI in 2024 as an upper-mid-range device. It has a Snapdragon 6 Gen 1 chipset, 8GB of RAM, and 128GB of storage, with Android 14 having been pre-installed at launch. Android 17 was the last promised update even though it wasn’t included in the initial roadmap Sony posted in September. 

The company says that Xperia 10 VI “does not support an Android 17 upgrade experience that we consider adequate” due to a “limitation” related to the phone’s storage. The exact reason isn’t entirely clear, but Sony says security updates will continue on as promised, and that other Xperia devices due to get Android 17 will no be affected.

	

Sony explains:

We announced at launch that the Xperia 10 VI would receive three Android OS upgrades. However, after a detailed technical assessment, we determined that due to limitations related to the device’s storage configuration, the Xperia 10 VI does not support an Android 17 upgrade experience that we consider adequate. Accordingly, we have decided not to make this upgrade available. We recognise that this falls short of our original announcement, and we wish to apologise for this change.

On the other hand, our security update commitment remains unchanged. Sony will continue to provide security updates for four years from the product’s launch date, as previously communicated.

This issue is specific to Xperia 10 VI’s technical specifications and will not impact other Xperia models.

It’s certainly an odd situation, and one that we don’t often see. While it’s not uncommon for Android phones to not be promised as many updates as they should recieve, it’s rare for a promised software update to be canceled outright.

title: Oppo confirms list of devices getting its Android 17 update, rollout starts this month
snippet: Oppo has officially revealed ColorOS 17, its Android 17 update, to global markets this week and, along with that, confirmed a list of devices poised to get the update. more…
fullText:
Oppo has officially revealed ColorOS 17, its Android 17 update, to global markets this week and, along with that, confirmed a list of devices poised to get the update.

ColorOS 17 is Oppo’s Android 17 update, and it has two main focuses – smooth performance, and AI. It’s also packed with Liquid Glass design elements, as if that should surprise anyone at this point. 

Oppo calls its Liquid Glass copy “Flow,” with the “Luminous Rendering Engine” powering animations that react to your touch. Oppo says:

ColorOS 17 reimagines how you interact with the system. It senses the pressure and direction of your touch, responding with fluid, elastic motion and nuanced lighting effects that make every interaction feel truly alive. With the all-new Unified Rendering Architecture, transitions between elements are more seamless and refined than ever.

Oppo says that ColorOS 17 is also faster and more reliable, touting 55% “more stable app launches” and 25% better app retention in memory. 

	

As with anything else in 2026, AI is a big part of the update, with Oppo continuing to build out features like AI Mind Space (similar to Pixel Screenshots and Nothing’s Essential Space), adding “AI Mind Pilot” as an agentic AI service, “AI Mind Suggest” as a proactive flight companion, an “AI Photo Agent” is a prompt-based photo editor.

Oppo says ColorOS 17 will start rolling out globally this month – October 29, to be exact – with over a dozen devices set to be updated before the month’s end and many more to be updated through the first quarter of 2027.

title: Apple’s new ‘Switch to Safari’ campaign details why you should ditch Chrome
snippet: Apple is kicking off a new campaign today to promote Safari’s benefits over Chrome. With a new “Switch to Safari” page on its website and a pair of new YouTube videos, Apple wants everyone to know Safari is “a more powerful and private browser than Chrome.” more…
fullText:
Apple is kicking off a new campaign today to promote Safari’s benefits over Chrome. With a new “Switch to Safari” page on its website and a pair of new YouTube videos, Apple wants everyone to know Safari is “a more powerful and private browser than Chrome.”

On the new website, Apple touts several advantages of Safari over Chrome, including better battery life, stronger privacy protections, and faster performance.

Safari offers up to 5 hours more video streaming on your Mac compared with Chrome.

title: iCloud+ keeps getting better, here’s what’s new for subscribers

fullText:
iCloud+ is best known for adding iCloud storage, but Apple keeps improving and expanding its suite of benefits for subscribers. Here’s everything new for iCloud+ added in the last few weeks.

iCloud+ additions include HomeKit Secure Video upgrades, free Apple TV and Arcade for many, higher AI usage limits, more

If you subscribe to iCloud+ or Apple One, you’re probably getting more benefits than you realize.

	

Beyond extra storage, iCloud+ includes features like Hide My Email, iCloud Private Relay, full Apple Invites access, and more.

Here’s everything new for iCloud+ subscribers added in the last few weeks:

HomeKit Secure Video upgrades: Ahead of new Home products launching this week, Apple has upgraded HomeKit Secure Video in several ways. iOS 27’s powerful new features include 4K support, generated video descriptions, clip searching, and noteworthy clips.

Custom Email Domain: If you run a small business or want to use custom emails for your family or for any other reason, iCloud+ lets you set up personalized addresses for domains you own. You were previously limited to three personalized email addresses, but now you can create up to 10 per domain.

Apple TV and Arcade added in 100+ countries: It doesn’t apply to the US, but iCloud+ subscribers in more than 100 countries now get Apple TV and Arcade thrown in at no additional cost. It’s a huge upgrade for many users that makes the service more of a no-brainer in supported territories.

Higher AI usage limits in iOS 27: Specifics are still unclear, but when Apple unveiled iOS 27, it said select iCloud+ plans would include higher usage limits for AI features. Few phones have been more anticipated than a foldable iPhone, but it’s finally here. The iPhone Duo was unveiled during Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 models.

Apple’s first foldable has a 5.4-inch outer screen, and it unfolds to show off its 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR screen. Apple Pencil support is coming later this year. title: LineageOS support finally comes to Pixel 10 and 10a lineup
snippet: After a protracted wait, LineageOS is now officially available for the entire Pixel 10 lineup and the more affordable Pixel 10a. more…
fullText:
After a protracted wait, LineageOS is now officially available for the entire Pixel 10 lineup and the more affordable Pixel 10a.

Over a year since its release, it’s great news that Pixel 10 owners now have the option to flash LineageOS on their devices, but the long wait is likely due to circumstances beyond the Lineage team’s control.

Google has made it harder for ROM projects in recent years, making it harder for projects like Lineage and Graphene, as the company is no longer sharing device trees and driver binaries. This coincided with the launch of Android 16, and so it has likely stalled some of the development for the last generation of hardware.

On top of that, delays to public kernel downloads for Pixel devices haven’t been ideal.

	

Some of this likely accounts for the delay in LineageOS builds for Pixel 10. At least the good news is that builds are now available for download on the same day LineageOS 24 was announced. This latest version is the Android 17 build for the custom ROM and comes with a number of changes to take better advantage of the enhancements added in early June 2026.

This release includes a whole host of Material 3 Expressive changes to the default app suite with a brand new “Canvas” image editor. Security patches are accounted for up to October 2026, meaning you are fully secure if you do prefer an AI-free experience with Lineage on your Pixel 10.

It’s worth noting that Pixel 10 Pro XL, 10 Pro Fold, and Pixel 10a builds are not yet live, but nightly Pixel 10 and 10 Pro builds are live right now.

title: Apple TV 4K and HomeView: The best and worst of $299
snippet: Wow, $299. That’s a very surprising price. For HomeView, Apple’s all-new smart display, $299 feels surprisingly affordable. For Apple TV 4K, $299 feels surprisingly painful. more…
fullText:
Wow, $299. That’s a very surprising price. For HomeView, Apple’s all-new smart display, $299 feels surprisingly affordable. For Apple TV 4K, $299 feels surprisingly painful.

HomeView for $299 feels like an invitation to try a new product category

HomeView looks like a hit. Without actually seeing or hearing it, the verdict is still out. What we can judge now is the pitch. 

In classic Apple fashion, the company is hardly the first to deliver a smart display. Yet HomeView appears to have the polish and consideration that an iPhone user would expect.

At $299, it seems Apple is pricing HomeView more as an invitation to try a new category of product. I’m intrigued.

Apple TV 4K for $299 feels like Apple already knows the customer

Then there’s the Apple TV 4K. At $299, it feels priced more like specialized hardware. Unlike HomeView, Apple TV 4K has a price history.

In 2021, Apple sold two Apple TV boxes: Apple TV HD for $149, and Apple TV 4K (2nd generation) for $179.

Both boxes ran tvOS with an App Store, but customers didn’t love that 4K support costed nearly $200.

By the end of the following year, Apple TV 4K (3rd generation) arrived in two flavors: 64GB with no Thread or Ethernet for $129, or 128GB with Thread and Ethernet for $149.

This was viewed as a great cost correction compared to the previous generation. Better hardware and a better price? That sounds too good to be true.

But it was true for a while. Then Apple raised prices on a number of existing products in June. You may recall Apple TV 4K being one of the more painful price jumps, both due to the percent increase and the age of the hardware.

The $129 model jumped to $199, and the $149 model jumped to $249.

Today’s Apple TV 4K replaces the $249 model with an even higher $299 price.

We’re now back to the original Apple TV starting price from 2007. Boy, what a relief when Apple switched from local storage to streaming with the vastly different Apple TV (2nd generation) puck for $99.

Apple TV 4K the best experience, but it’s for fewer people now

Anyway, things are different in 2026. You can literally buy a 65-inch 4K LED TV with the Apple TV app (and all the other streaming apps) built-in for $299.

Where does that leave the Apple TV 4K? It’s increasingly positioned not as a way to add streaming apps to your TV, but as a very particular way to bring the full Apple experience to your TV.

But did Apple get the feature set for the price right?

Adding mics to the box itself is a nice touch, especially since other set-top boxes already do this. There’s also the chip upgrade.

Another big new feature is support for creating a home theater experience beyond stereo speaker output with a pair of big HomePod speakers and a pair of new HomePod mini 2 speakers. That’s a $1300 experience between the set-top box and four speakers.

Personally, I’ve stayed on the Apple TV 4K (2nd-gen) from 2021 without any complaints. I don’t know how much I’ll use Siri AI from my TV, but having it come to the box I already own is a nice surprise.

A specialized home theater experience isn’t a priority in the budget right now, so I’m plenty happy with my 55-inch 4K LED that costed me $168 on sale from Hisense. It’s not the absolute best TV I’ve ever owned, but it’s plenty enough for me. Attaching a $299 Apple TV 4K to it would almost feel wrong.

	

But if a premium home theater experience is at the top of your priorities and cost isn’t a concern, Apple TV 4K at $299 is a sure upgrade over built-in TV experiences for Apple users.

For now, I’m just grateful that I’m getting most of that experience from a purchase made years ago.

Hopefully there’s an Apple TV option in the future that feels less overpowered and overpriced needs and budgets like mine in the future. At this point, even a version without the $59 Siri Remote in the box would feel more palatable.

Share your thoughts in the comments.
