title: Bluesky wants to make it easier to buy, sell, and fundraise on the network
snippet: The executives argued that advertising isn’t the only path to monetization, and that there are alternative models that are feasible when it comes to monetization.
fullText:
Bluesky plans to introduce payments in the coming months, a first step in its strategy to make money without relying on advertising. CEO Toni Schneider and COO Rose Wang outlined the plans Thursday at TechCrunch Disrupt, explaining how the company hopes to build on the commerce and fundraising activity already happening on its decentralized social network.

“People are actually selling things, fundraising very successfully, supporting each other on the network,” Schneider said. “We want to make that easier, and the way we’re going to do this is if you see something on the network that you like and support, you can support that monetarily, and we want to do it in a way that works for Bluesky and for all the other apps out there as well, so that it works across the entire network.”

Schneider, the former CEO of Automattic, took the reins of the company in March after longtime CEO Jay Graber stepped down. He said, while onstage, that he was surprised by the reaction to his appointment, with some users joking that it marked the beginning of the end for the platform. Those comments reflected fears that a leadership change would bring unwanted changes to Bluesky.

Schneider said he understands that users can leave Bluesky for another platform if the company introduces features or changes they dislike, a reality that he said keeps the leadership team accountable as it prepares to introduce monetization in the coming months.

The executives argued that advertising isn’t the only viable business model for a social network. 

Image Credits:Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch

“I think there’s a story around monetization that feels like advertising is the inevitable thing we have to do that will ruin the network,” Wang said. “What was really promising about having Toni join us is he built at WordPress Automatic a $10 billion business where a billion of it goes back to the parent company and the rest of it goes to the ecosystem.”

Wang also pointed to Bluesky’s status as a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), which she said puts the company’s mission at the center of its business strategy.

“Yes, we need to make money, but because of our infrastructure, we cannot lock people in,” Wang said. “And so the thing that really matters for us is the people who are creating value on the networks these days are the ones who are getting the value that is coming in or the money that’s coming in. And I kind of think of it as like feudal society where we’re working for a few landlords and they dictate everything, and then we have to pay up our dues as tariffs.”

Bluesky aims to give users ownership of their digital identities and control over their networks while creating a more open internet where value and revenue can flow directly to the people who generate them.

“First, we’ll start with payments, but I think it’s about disrupting the actual infrastructure layer, which is what we’re doing, and not just building another app,” Wang said.

“People are actually selling things, fundraising very successfully, supporting each other on the network,” Schneider said. “We want to make that easier, and the way we’re going to do this is if you see something on the network that you like and support, you can support that monetarily, and we want to do it in a way that works for Bluesky and for all the other apps out there as well, so that it works across the entire network.”

title: Apple unveils new HomeView smart display: pre-order today for $299
snippet: Apple today officially unveiled its new HomeView smart display. HomeView features a 7-inch square display and comes in two versions: one with a speaker base and another for wall mounting. You can pre-order HomeView today for $299. It will start arriving to customers on November 13. Here’s everything you need to know about HomeView. more…
fullText:
Apple today officially unveiled its new HomeView smart display. HomeView features a 7-inch square display and comes in two versions: one with a speaker base and another for wall mounting.

You can pre-order HomeView today for $299. It will start arriving to customers on November 13.

Here’s everything you need to know about HomeView.

Apple HomeView: Features, specs, price, and more

HomeView features a 7-inch Liquid Retina display that’s connected to a domed speaker base with a stainless steel hinge with tilt support. The display features Apple’s True Tone technology and 500 nits of brightness. It can also dim to 0.3 nits, making it great for a nightstand. 

There’s also a separate wall-mounted version of HomeView. This model can be “attached to a wall using three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home, with options for self-installation or professional installation.” 

Here are the details on those wall-mounting options from Apple: 

HomeView (Wall Mounted) will be available with a choice of three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home. Power Mount USB‑C Wall Connector, available starting at $59.95 (U.S.), and Power Mount AC Wired, available starting at $79.95 (U.S.), can be ordered starting today from apple.com/store and in the Apple Store app. Power Mount PoE Wired will be available starting in early 2027 for $129.95 (U.S.).

Apple says the HomeView interface will intelligently adjust based on how far away you are. It will show “simpler information that’s viewable from across the room” as well as “richer detail” as you step closer. 

HomeView can also recognize up to six different people and deliver a “personalized experience” for each one. This includes a personalized Home Screen with apps and widgets. “Personal content stays private from others, while shared photo albums and music can be easily enjoyed by everyone in a household, including guests,” Apple says. 

There is a collection of “playful and informative” faces for HomeView: 

Users can personalize HomeView with a collection of playful and informative faces that display information at a glance, taking full advantage of the vibrant Liquid Retina display. The Photos face brings cherished memories to life with stunning Portrait-style depth effects that keep the subject sharp while creating a beautifully blurred foreground and background. 

By selecting a shared album, users can turn HomeView into a living photo frame that loved ones near and far can help fill. The Flow face dynamically responds to physical presence and movement, transforming HomeView into a piece of interactive art. And even Snoopy comes to life on HomeView, with animations that reflect the time of day, the weather, sporting events, and holiday moments.

HomeView supports Siri AI. Apple says that users with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad can tap into personal context. Users without an Apple Intelligence-capable device can still use Siri AI on HomeView for world knowledge and music discovery. 

For audio quality, Apple says HomeView has a “custom-engineered acoustic system” with two full-range drivers in the display, plus a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators.

Here are some more HomeView tidbits: 

It has a Center Stage camera for FaceTime calls. 

There’s a “Home Modular” face that gives easy access to smart home accessories. The “Home Camera” face can livestream up to nine video feeds at once.

HomeView isn’t available in the European Union because Siri AI isn’t available there either. Apple says it is “working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward.” 

The table-top version of HomeView is available in silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray. The wall-mounted version is available in space gray and silver. You can pre-order both today for $299, with availability beginning November 13.

title: Apple Store is down ahead of iPhone Duo preorder rush
snippet: In keeping with tradition, Apple has taken down the Apple Store this morning ahead of the iPhone Duo going up for preorder. If you are waiting to buy the new Apple foldable, be sure to log on at 5 AM Eastern Time. All reports point to constrained supply and relatively high demand, so everyone is anticipating that Apple will run out of launch day stock very quickly indeed. fullText:
In keeping with tradition, Apple has taken down the Apple Store this morning ahead of the iPhone Duo going up for preorder. If you are waiting to buy the new Apple foldable, be sure to log on at 5 AM Eastern Time.

All reports point to constrained supply and relatively high demand, so everyone is anticipating that Apple will run out of launch day stock very quickly indeed. If you want a Duo for launch day, on October 23, you need to be ready to buy at 5 AM.

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first foldable, featuring a 7.6-inch inner display and a 5.4-inch outer display when closed. Apple has engineered the product to feature a minimal crease when unfolded, aided by a custom hinge design and a nano-texture matte finish on the inner display. 

It is powered by Apple’s latest A20 Pro chip, and should offer computational performance in the ballpark of the iPhone 18 Pro line. The cameras are a downgrade though, due to the device’s thinner design when unfolded, and the Duo only has Touch ID rather than Face ID biometrics.

The Duo comes in two colors, Night Sky and Star White, and starts at $1999 for the entry-level 256 GB model.

iPhone Duo will launch with iOS 27.1, which will include a bunch of software UI optimisations for the product’s unusual form factor. This includes a new vertical bar where all the controls in updated apps appear along the right-edge of the phone, making them easy to tap with your thumb. 

All of Apple’s apps have also been updated to smoothly expand between the outer display and the larger inner display, and app developers are also submitting compatibility updates as we speak.

While foldables in general make up a small percentage of overall smartphone sales, Apple’s entrance into the category is expected to make a mark. We think the Duo will be a big hit, at least relatively to the competition. 

Whether Apple can manufacture enough of them will be the problem, at least for the first few months. Reports have indicated Apple’s suppliers will ship about 7-10 million Duos for the rest of 2026.

title: Apple says beloved MacBook is now ‘obsolete,’ more products too
snippet: Apple has just updated its list of vintage and obsolete products, adding the final model of the beloved 12-inch MacBook to the “obsolete” list alongside two other products. more…
fullText:
Apple has just updated its list of vintage and obsolete products, adding the final model of the beloved 12-inch MacBook to the “obsolete” list alongside two other products.

All 12-inch MacBook models are now obsolete, as iPad 6 and BeatsX join list too

Today Apple marked three additional products as “obsolete” on its website.

The company keeps a public list of vintage and obsolete products here. It’s regularly updated with new additions based on how long ago a product stopped being available for purchase.

Essentially, if a product stopped being on sale from Apple 5 or more years ago, it’s considered “vintage.” This means Apple will still service the product, but parts availability may be limited.

If a product stopped being sold 7 or more years ago, it’s marked “obsolete.” Obsolete products are no longer eligible for repairs or any other servicing from Apple.

The latest obsolete products include:

MacBook (Retina, 12-inch, 2017)

iPad (6th generation) in Wi-Fi and Wi-Fi + Cellular models

BeatsX in a variety of colors, including Burned Red, Defiant Black-Red, Deep Black, Pure White, and Sky Blue

If you own any of these products, Apple will no longer be able to service them.

	

The most notable addition is the MacBook, as the 2017 model is the last one Apple produced before the line was discontinued. The 2015 and 2016 models were already on the obsolete list.

While the 12-inch MacBook was pitched by Apple as a type of MacBook Air successor, it never took off with consumers despite having a loyal base of fans who loved it.

title: Apple wins early access to OpenAI documents and employee testimony in trade secrets lawsuit
snippet: Judge Edward Davila today granted some of Apple’s requests for expedited discovery in its trade secrets lawsuit against former employees, OpenAI, and io Products. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Judge Edward Davila today granted some of Apple’s requests for expedited discovery in its trade secrets lawsuit against former employees, OpenAI, and io Products. Here are the details.

A bit of background

A few months ago, Apple filed a trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products.

In a nutshell, Apple says Liu and Tan improperly accessed or used confidential information about its products and technologies to help advance OpenAI’s consumer hardware development efforts. Apple also accuses the defendants of improperly obtaining information from other Apple employees during recruitment interviews.

You can read more about Apple’s original filing here.

As part of the lawsuit, Apple asked Judge Edward Davila to issue a preliminary injunction to prevent the defendants from further embedding the alleged trade secrets in their hardware development while the case plays out.

Apple also requested expedited discovery, seeking early access to internal documents, forensic evidence, and testimony from OpenAI employees to better understand the extent of the alleged misappropriation and support its injunction request.

OpenAI opposed the motion, arguing that Apple’s demands were overly broad and that expedited discovery was unnecessary given that the regular process was about to begin.

Which brings us to today.

Judge partially grants Apple’s requests

In a decision issued today, Judge Davila granted most of Apple’s requests, while rejecting others and postponing a decision on those he considered overly broad.

That includes ordering the defendants to turn over several categories of documents and evidence, including:

All forensic images that Defendants have already collected in connection with the subject matter of Apple’s claims, including those [examined by OpenAI’s forensic expert];

All documents used to guide or conduct the interviews of candidates from Apple for OpenAI’s Consumer Hardware Products Group, […] including checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts; and all documents, including Technical Deep Dive presentations or other technical presentations, summarizing or otherwise memorializing the content of those interviews with Apple employees or any reference to any Apple technology or parts.

All LINE conversations between Mr. Liu and Ms. Peng since January 1, 2026, including the conversations that include the messages cited in [a previous filing made by the defendants]

Additionally, Judge Davila authorized Apple to depose Liu, Tan, and Yu-Ting “Alyssa” Peng, as well as corporate representatives from OpenAI and io Products.

On the flip side, Judge Davila rejected Apple’s request for expedited access to OpenAI’s research and development documents regarding metal finishes, power management, and battery functionality for consumer hardware products. Instead, he decided that these will be addressed through the regular discovery process.

Finally, he postponed a series of decisions involving what Apple described as “Apple Originated Information,” finding Apple’s definition “amorphous as currently defined.” On that point, Apple has five days to consult with the defendants and submit a narrower definition to the court if it wishes to take another crack at those requests.

The decision also addressed whether the expedited depositions will count toward the limits imposed by federal discovery rules, as well as the deadlines for producing documents and conducting depositions, and you can read it in full below:

title: YouTube reportedly ‘looking’ into adding audiobooks to Premium
snippet: Based on a recent report, YouTube is apparently considering adding audiobooks as a new medium alongside music and video. more…
fullText:
Based on a recent report, YouTube is apparently considering adding audiobooks as a new medium alongside music and video.

According to a report by The Wall Street Journal, YouTube is “looking” into audiobooks for a future addition to the app. There’s little detail as to when it could become a concrete feature, or whether it would be offered as a standalone benefit.

The report does mention that Google is considering offering it with YouTube Premium, which costs $16/month. It would join ad-free music playback with YouTube music, in addition to the main selling point – ad-free videos.

	

YouTube has seemingly not confirmed the possibility. It wouldn’t be unheard of, considering Spotify and other major platforms have partnered with audiobook services to offer users a little more than just music.

	

While it isn’t entirely the same thing, Google Play Books’ YouTube channel has been a dedicated spot for audiobook previews, and this integration would just make it easier to connect the two products.

It also wouldn’t be the first time YouTube has donned another hat. Shorts was seen as a direct way to compete with TikTok, and it’s become a major part of the app for the company. But the YouTube Music app might be a better fit for audiobooks, rather than the main video hub.

What do you think? Are audiobooks something you’d want to see bundled into YouTube Premium?

Elon Musk promised a flying car. And the Tesla Roadster did exactly that.

Tesla demonstrated its next-generation Roadster at an event in Waco, Texas, where the electric supercar drove upside down, briefly flew, and accelerated to 60mph in under a second. It was an impressive demonstration of a car that likely will come with some heavy caveats and restrictions if it ever goes into production.

The event was less than 30 minutes and felt more like a stunt show than a product reveal. Indeed, there was no mention of price, release date, or other such mundane details. Musk promised the hypercar would go into production in 2028, but after nearly nine years who’s counting. The people were here to see a car fly, and that’s what Tesla gave them.

1/5

First, the Roadster drove up a very tall, multi-story ramp, using its incredible downforce to cling to the vertical roadway. When it reached the top of the ramp, it flipped around using its cold-gas thrusters to bring it gently back down to earth. The car uses a fan-based suction system, supplied by SpaceX and mounted underneath the vehicle, which is capable of generating up to two Gs of suction force.

Next, the Roadster flew over the rest of Tesla’s lineup, including the Model 3, Model Y, Cybertruck, Semi, and Cybercab — doing what Tesla VP for Engineering Lars Moravy called “a kick flip” in the process. Musk explained that it features attitude-control thrusters as well as main thrusters at the rear, giving the Roadster rocket-like capabilities.

“So it can basically fly like a rocket,” Musk said. “And it could do rolls. It could do, like, crazy gymnastics. Whatever you want, really. Now, I should say that this is not necessarily a safety-optimized car. But it takes the fun meter to 11 out of 10.”

The Roadster two ultra-high pressure air tanks with a combined volume of 600 liters, containing approximately 250 kilograms of air, and uses 10 nozzles to execute its maneuvers. The Roadster can even recharge its own tank, without requiring a specialized chemical propellant. The stored compressed air supplies the thrust needed to lift the car and perform the demonstrated maneuvers.

Musk claimed “This will be an actual car that’s on the roads” — though later the company admitted it would not be road legal. This seems obvious, of course. Imagine having to satisfy strict regulatory requirements from the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. The Roadster could go into production in 2028, as Musk promised — or it could be another decade of missed deadlines and broken promises. Again, who cares? Car flew.

As for the Roadster itself, Musk called it “the last best driver’s car.” Moravy said that Tesla drew inspiration from aerospace designs such as the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft. It’s a two-seater, with seats molded directly into the chassis. Its steering and driving controls use steer-by-wire technology, including a steer-by-wire yoke, brakes, and throttle. The rear of the car features the thrusters and fans housed around the diffuser area. And it has a retractable rear wing for added downforce.

1/7

Tesla has also said that the Roadster can accelerate from 0-60mph in less than a second. And during the event, the company claimed it did so in 0.81 seconds. Musk explained that increasing the applied force while reducing the vehicle’s mass help boost acceleration. In fact, Musk says the production Roadster should improve on the demonstrated result, although he acknowledged the extreme forces involved and the need to avoid subjecting occupants to extreme acceleration.

“You’ve got to crack halfway to the speed of sound, I think,” Musk teased. “Mach 0.5. Maybe a little higher.”

After the event, Tesla updated its website with details about the three distinct performance tiers for the next-generation Roadster, outlining how its controversial cold-gas thruster systems scale across the lineup:

Performance (Road Ready): The entry-level variant seats two passengers and relies on an active aerodynamics package paired with a multi-mode suction system to maximize downforce on and off the track. It claims a 0–60 mph time under 1.6 seconds and a target range exceeding 300 miles.

Thrust (Race Ready): Also a two-seater, this mid-tier version pairs the multi-mode suction system with rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters. The additional propulsion cuts the vehicle’s 0–60 mph acceleration to under 0.9 seconds. Tesla says this configuration will be in “limited release.”

Rocket (Air Ready): The single-seat flagship model expands the hardware to a full perimeter-mounted array of cold-gas thrusters. In addition to driving forward and upward acceleration, the thrusters enable lateral and rotational movement in midair — enabling the short, low-altitude stunts showcased at the event. This top-spec version reaches a top speed over 230 mph and pushes 0–60 mph acceleration to under 0.59 seconds. Tesla says this version will be “invite only,” but also “not approved for public road use.”

The next-gen Roadster certainly took the scenic route in getting here. A prototype version was announced as a “one more thing” style surprise during the 2017 Tesla Semi event. The specs sounded ludicrous even back then: 0-60 mph in 1.9 seconds, a top speed over 250 mph, a 200 kWh battery delivering up to 620 miles of range, and a $200,000 starting price tag. Musk said deliveries would start in 2020, which sounded perfectly doable at the time.

Early adopters quickly threw down $50,000 deposits (or $250,000 for the limited Founders Series), effectively interest-free loans to help fund Tesla’s scaling ambitions. But then Tesla seemed to forget about the Roadster, as cementing its status as the ultimate vaporware. Production deadlines slipped as Tesla prioritized mass-market vehicles like the Model Y, while also wrestling with the overly complicated Cybertruck. Occasionally, when Musk would remember that the Roadster existed, he would up the ante about its capabilities. This culminated in the “SpaceX package” that would equip the supercar with cold-gas thrusters, bestowing hover powers and a 0-60 time under one second.

Musk has also sought to downplay the Roadster’s significance, calling it a “small potato situation” that will not “move the needle in a major way financially.” He’s framed the supercar more as a joint engineering collaboration between Tesla and SpaceX, even questioning whether it’s “even a car anymore” given its experimental nature. Some analysts theorize that the decision to re-release the Roadster is an attempt to set the stage for a rumored Tesla-SpaceX merger.

Tesla’s failure to bring the Roadster to market allowed other automakers to slip past the company with their own hyper-powered EVs. Rimac has smashed performance records with the Nevera, Porsche has refined electric performance with the Taycan, and Chinese giants like BYD are producing track-ready supercars at a fraction of the cost. The Roadster is no longer shocking the world as an impossible prototype; it’s playing catch-up to an industry that spent nine years building what Tesla merely rendered.

But then again, none of those cars flew.

title: Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style
snippet: The new car used thrusters to leap over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 at a demo in Texas.
fullText:
Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.”

Musk showed off the car at an event outside Waco, Texas, with a demonstration that saw the car use a mixture of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and ease itself to a landing on the pavement below. The car also used the thrusters to lift itself over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 while in motion.

“This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.”

Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price. Tesla will offer it in three trims. The first is “Performance,” which Tesla describes as “road ready.” It seats two, has active aerodynamics, and features a “multi-mode suction system for next-level performance on and off the track.” The second trim is “Thrust,” which is “race ready” and seats two, and has rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters that enable sub-one-second 0-to-60 mph acceleration. The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car.

All three trims will have 300 miles of range and be capable of speeds exceeding 230 miles per hour.

Tesla’s website showed Thursday the company is taking reservations for the car, charging $50,000 just to reserve the Performance, and $250,000 for Thrust. The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.”  

Tesla Roadster-starmanImage Credits:Tesla

Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair. The air tank can be recharged, he said. “Every usable void in the car is packed with Carbon Fiber Overwrapped Pressure Vessels (COPVs),” Tesla wrote in a post on X, referring to the type of pressure vessel that has been at the root of multiple SpaceX rocket explosions. The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels.

Musk also said at the event that Tesla may try to jump the Snake River Canyon — the site of Evel Knievel’s famous attempt to cross the gorge in a steam-powered rocket.

Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster.

“If you buy a Ferrari, safety is not the number one goal. I say, if safety is your number one goal, do not buy the Roadster,” he said on a podcast earlier this year. Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said.

“This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX Engineers working closely together to make something you haven’t seen in any movie, better than any James Bond car,” Musk said at the event. “I’ve never seen anything like this. You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’”

Tesla roadster eventImage Credits:Tesla

Musk had previously claimed that the car “will be very different from what was shown previously” and promised the demo would be the “most exciting, whether it works or not, demo ever of any product.” 

The design changes were notable. The car, shown in stark white, now has a more angular design reminiscent of a Lamborghini or the famous Lotus Esprit used by the James Bond character in “The Spy Who Loved Me” — a car Musk owns, which was on display at the event.

In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet.

“Our design language has evolved since the last reveal: from S3XY to Cybertruck, Cybercab & Optimus,” the company wrote. 

Tesla held the event almost nine years to the day after the company first revealed the second-generation Roadster, a modernized take on its first-ever car. Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years. Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car. Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions.

Musk first talked about adding thrusters to the car in 2018. “SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car,” he wrote on Twitter that year. “These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …” 

But the Roadster project took a back seat. In 2018, Tesla suffered through what Musk eventually dubbed “production hell” with the Model 3 sedan. The company then moved on to other projects like the Model Y SUV, which became the best-selling vehicle in the world, and the Cybertruck, which was a commercial flop by Tesla’s own standards. Along the way, Musk delayed the new Roadster in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024.

As more time passed following the launch of those new vehicles, Musk started talking about the second-generation Roadster again. Late last year, he said on Joe Rogan’s podcast that he wanted to reveal it by the end of 2025. One week later, at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026. Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again.

“Like, I could say I was just kidding,” he said at the time. Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again. It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay.

These repeated delays caused a number of high-profile customers to speak out over the years, including YouTuber Marques Brownlee and OpenAI head Sam Altman.

“They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028,” Brownlee posted Thursday. “This is a prank, right?”

title: iPhone Duo now available to pre-order, prices start at $1,999
snippet: Apple’s first-ever foldable iPhone is now available for pre-order. You can head to Apple’s website or the Apple Store app this morning to place your iPhone Duo pre-order, with the first orders arriving in one week on October 23. more…
fullText:
Apple’s first-ever foldable iPhone is now available for pre-order. You can head to Apple’s website or the Apple Store app this morning to place your iPhone Duo pre-order, with the first orders arriving in one week on October 23.

Apple is bringing the Apple Store back online in waves, so if you don’t have the option to pre-order iPhone Duo just yet, keep waiting. 

As a refresher, iPhone Duo features a 5.4-inch outer display that unfolds into a 7.6-inch inner display. It’s powered by Apple’s A20 Pro chip. It has a dual-camera system on the back, including a 48MP Main camera and a 48MP Ultra Wide camera. There’s a Center Stage camera on the front, as well as a FaceTime camera underneath the inner display.

Here’s Apple on some of the software optimizations for the foldable iPhone Duo:

The expansive display on iPhone Duo supercharges productivity with Split View multitasking and seamless app switching, and a reimagined yet familiar iOS experience introduces entirely new ways to interact with iPhone.

iOS also adapts to content on iPhone Duo by reacting as it folds, reorienting when turned to the side, and switching to the appropriate display when flipped over. iPhone Duo can also enter StandBy on either the outer or inner display — even when it’s not charging — turning the device into a photo frame, a hub for widgets, a clock, and more.

	

iPhone Duo is available in two colors: star white and night sky. Pricing starts at $1,999 for the 256GB model.

title: LineageOS 24 launches based on Android 17 with app redesigns and simple flash tool
snippet: LineageOS 24 is now official, with the latest builds rolling out based on Android 17, bringing a surprise early release alongside a fresh coat of Material Design 3 Expressive paint, new WebUSB flashing tools, and more. more…
fullText:
LineageOS 24 is now official, with the latest builds rolling out based on Android 17, bringing a surprise early release alongside a fresh coat of Material Design 3 Expressive paint, new WebUSB flashing tools, and more.

Announced in a dedicated and detailed blog post, LineageOS 24 arrives just ahead of a major milestone for the custom ROM project, which celebrates its 10th anniversary on December 24, 2026.

Compared to previous release cycles, the team is well ahead of schedule this time around. Releasing earlier than anticipated following Android 17’s initial June launch, LineageOS 24 gives those running existing builds the opportunity to upgrade to Google’s latest OS version. The release lands as LineageOS 24.0 and incorporates security patches from August 2025 up through October 2026 across supported branches.

While moving to Android 17 is notable alone, there are some other changes that are key to LineageOS 24.

	

One of the biggest headline changes in this release is a heavy focus on app design refreshes. Almost all of the core Lineage apps have been updated to Material Design 3 Expressive, highlighted by a brand-new built-in image editor called Canvas, which handles all the image editing regular stuff like basic cropping, white balance, and filters to pair nicely with Glimpse and Aperture. 

There’s also a major visual overhaul to the Updater, which now supports streamed updates by default to drastically cut down installation times on A/B devices. 

LineageOS 24’s music player, Twelve, has even faster load times for large media libraries, improved Jellyfin support, and a dedicated tab for your most-played tracks. This player was introduced back with LineageOS 22.

Not to be left out, the default browser Jelly now supports PWA-like apps using a new shortcut. This could be huge for those not wanting to install apps from third-party stores.

Installing LineageOS 24 is also getting a bit simpler for those usually not confident in flashing custom ROMs. The team is launching new WebUSB-based flash tools directly via the browser for common installation processes like ADB Fastboot, Amlogic Burn, and Samsung Odin protocols. While standard device wiki guides remain the default and fully supported path, these optional web tools help streamline the process for users looking to avoid extra desktop software.

On the maintenance side, LineageOS is formally restricting future builds for older devices running Linux Kernel versions 4.4 and 4.9. While these legacy kernels can no longer be submitted for LineageOS 23.2 or 24.0 builds, they will remain supported on LineageOS 22.2 with ongoing monthly security patches. Meanwhile, the team has expanded SoC-specific common kernels and commonized legacy device shims to simplify maintenance across popular chips from Qualcomm and Amlogic.

Rollouts will begin hitting a growing selection of supported devices in the coming weeks as maintainers bring them up to compliance. To check if your device is ready or to follow the upgrade path, you can head over to the official LineageOS Wiki.

title: World Timekeepers Decide to Kill the Leap Second
snippet: Doing away with the leap second might prevent time-related computer anomalies in the future.
fullText:
Human timekeeping rests on two main clocks, and they don’t always run at the same speed. For decades, the solution was the leap second, a minor adjustment added to international time to keep atomic accuracy aligned with the Earth’s natural motion. But on Thursday, the General Conference on Weights and Measures, or the CGPM (abbreviated from its French name), voted to abolish the leap second, closing a long-standing chapter in global time sync.

Most modern clocks rely on Coordinated Universal Time, a hybrid system caught between atomic time, which flows at a near-perfectly constant rate, and astronomical time, which fluctuates as the Earth’s rotation speeds up and slows down. To bridge the gap, UTC periodically inserted a leap second to keep pace with the planet. But reconciling physical planetary shifts with precise digital systems ultimately created more technical disruptions than it solved.

Breaking time

Computers are sensitive when it comes to timekeeping. The last few times we added a leap second to UTC — in 2012, 2015 and 2016 – some computer systems couldn’t handle it. Of the three instances, 2012 was the worst, as adding a leap second caused issues that crashed websites and software platforms, such as Reddit, LinkedIn and Mozilla.

			

More from CNET

The speed of Earth’s rotation experiences small changes all the time. While we can’t predict exactly how fast Earth will rotate in the future, the conference wrote that there’s a 30% chance we’ll have to add a negative leap second by 2035 to keep UTC aligned with rotational time. 

If adding a regular leap second was trouble, imagine what adding a negative leap second could do. The conference doesn’t want to risk finding out. So, potential future computer anomalies caused by UTC changes are a major reason why the leap second is going away. 

“Industrial users and the synchronization needs of national critical infrastructures, for example, transportation, energy distribution, telecommunication, and space projects, require UTC to be continuous without any future adjustment,” the group’s resolution reads.

Moving forward

The official death of the leap second will be May 20, 2027, when continuous UTC becomes effective. A continuous UTC means that no more leap seconds, negative or otherwise, will be added to UTC going forward. This also means that UTC and rotational time will begin to drift apart. 

The CGPM noted that allowing time measurements to differ by up to an hour will keep UTC stable for several centuries.

This means in the future, when it’s noon, the sun might not be at its highest in the sky. But, considering we’ve only added 27 leap seconds since the concept was introduced in 1972, any changes that occur within our lifetimes will probably be very small. 

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Julian Dossett
						

						

							Writer						
					

											

								

											Julian is a contributor and former staff writer at CNET.

title: Governments are hacking people with ‘zero-click’ spyware by showing them online ads
snippet: The digital rights unit found evidence that dozens of devices at media organization Al Jazeera were hacked after being shown malicious online ads.
fullText:
Security researchers at digital rights unit The Citizen Lab say government spyware makers are abusing global advertising networks to target and hack devices by serving malicious online adverts.

A new report published Thursday by the University of Toronto lab, which investigates surveillance and digital rights abuses, said an Israeli company called Discover-Tech allows spyware makers to use its advertising platform to target specific people or devices almost anywhere in the world with spyware capable of invisibly stealing their data.

The researchers say Discover-Tech presents itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but instead serves as a “bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem.”

Citizen Lab said at least two makers of zero-click spyware, Candiru and Bindecy, used Discover-Tech’s platform to target people. Both of these spyware makers provide surveillance products that can infect devices without the victim having to open a message or click on a link. 

The researchers found that one attack affected at least 45 Windows computers at media organization Al Jazeera. The devices were apparently hacked in 2024 and 2025 via Candiru’s spyware after being exposed to online ads packed with malicious code.

Citizen Lab said it wasn’t clear which governments were behind the attacks, but said this is the first confirmation of zero-click government-backed spyware attacks being delivered through online ads, potentially putting a vast number of devices around the world at risk of being targeted and hacked.

“There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a Citizen Lab senior researcher, ahead of the report’s release.

Hackers have long sought ways to abuse access to advertising networks, in part because of their ability to reach almost any internet-connected device in the world. Ad networks are designed to help advertisers target certain kinds of people, devices, and organizations with specific ads, but they can also be abused to target specific individuals or devices with malicious code. 

While such so-called “malvertising” attacks are not new, using online ads to allow powerful government spyware to silently hack into devices is a notable escalation.

Security and privacy experts have for years encouraged people to install ad-blockers to prevent ads from being displayed on desktop and mobile screens, including within apps. But the ubiquity of online advertising makes it difficult to escape the industry’s clutches entirely.

Image Credits:Citizen Lab (screenshot)

The researchers said Discover-Tech’s platform, which the company calls Controlium, left some of its source code exposed on its login pages, allowing the researchers to recreate its web-based control panel dashboard without needing to log in. The researchers say the web dashboard “appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements.”

Citizen Lab also found that Discover-Tech’s site had a publicly accessible portion that allowed the researchers to download reams of user login records for the Controlium dashboard without needing a password. Some login details belonged to at least two employees of spyware maker Candiru, as well as some from Bindecy.

The researchers also found billions of ad bidding records left exposed on Discover-Tech’s website, which showed that its ads had ultimately been displayed across tens of thousands of mobile apps and websites between March and June 2026.

The bidding records show that the ads were shown on devices used by militaries, governments, critical infrastructure, and national cyber agencies. However, it’s unclear if the displayed ads resulted in a compromise or infection. 

Security researchers with ad quality platform Confiant, which worked with Citizen Lab to investigate, said they found evidence that potentially malicious ads were similarly shown on devices on the networks of the International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.

Citizen Lab’s Marczak said Discover-Tech is “surely just the tip of the iceberg,” and urged people to take defensive action. 

“If you might be targeted based on who you are or what you do, it’s time to disable ad tracking on your devices or even block ads altogether,” said Marczak.

Al Jazeera did not respond to a request for comment about the hacks. Neither did Discover-Tech, and Candiru maker Integrity Labs could not be reached for comment.

Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security.

fullText:
Google Home is getting a fresh update with improvements to reordering your favorite devices, redesigned controls for third-party smart home devices, and some much-needed fixes for Gemini commands.

I can’t speak for everyone else, but the Favorites tab in Home probably accounts for nearly all of my interactions with the app, which is why it’s so exciting to see Google making some big changes here. This month’s changelog suggests any “instability” seen while dragging and dropping tiles across your Favorites view has been smoothed out, and as someone who has absolutely given up on trying to manage that page in the past, I couldn’t be more grateful. 

Of course, if you prefer controlling your lights or speakers with voice commands, you’ll know it’s Gemini that really needs some attention within Home. Google says it’s rolling out a bunch of fixes to how Gemini works with its smart home app, including more reliable “stop” commands to prevent misinterpretations and easier-to-read answers on smart displays. For my money, though, it’s the move to implement “more natural ways” to stop your conversation with Gemini that’s the highlight of the bunch, allowing you to quickly end your chat with a simple “thank you” to cease talking and close the mic.

Other Gemini fixes include the ability to better differentiate between relaxing music and ambient sounds — you’d think AI would know the difference between soothing spa music and white noise without a specific update, but alas — and consistent temperature units for weather based on the preference set within your Home settings. Outside of Gemini, you’ll find large smoke alarm banners within the app, complete with event time information, a more responsive progress bar when scrubbing along paused video on Android, and Matter control for Phillips Hue lights with existing bridges.

title: Mafia, Horizon Forbidden West and More Games Are Coming to PlayStation Plus Soon
snippet: A few other scare-tastic games, like Poppy Playtime: Chapter 2, are also coming to the service in time for Halloween as well.
fullText:
PlayStation Plus is dressing up as a gangster this month. It’s not the most Halloween move the service could make, but I’m kind of into it.

There’s something very autumnal to me about mafia films and, therefore, the Mafia game series. Maybe it’s the muted color palette in some films, like the shades of brown throughout the Godfather, or all the suits and coats everyone wears that make me think of cooler weather. Either way, it feels fitting to me that Mafia: The Old Country, with its tale of organized crime in the hills of Sicily, is coming to PlayStation Plus this month.

PlayStation Plus, which is Sony’s version of Xbox Game Pass, offers a large, constantly expanding library of games. Subscribers can choose from the Essential, Extra and Premium tiers, each with unique perks and benefits. Starting at $11 per month, the plans give subscribers access to monthly games and rewards, and each month, all subscribers can access a handful of games at no additional charge. 

			

More from CNET

Here are all the games PlayStation Plus Premium and Extra subscribers can play soon. All games will be available to those PlayStation Plus subscribers on Oct. 20, unless otherwise noted.

Mafia: The Old Country

The fourth entry in the Mafia series is a prequel, which means it doesn’t require you to have any knowledge of the previous games. You play a man named Enzo as he becomes embroiled in organized crime in Sicily in the early 1900s. You will find shootouts, horse races and more in this sepia-toned crime game.

This sequel to Horizon Zero Dawn sees the main character Aloy, head west to find a cure for a mysterious plague that kills everyone it infects. While she travels this new frontier, you’ll reunite with old friends, encounter a war between rival factions and fight even more giant feral machines. 

Poppy Playtime: Chapter 2

Coming to PlayStation Plus on Oct. 27.

It wouldn’t be October without at least one horror game. After freeing Poppy in the first entry of this series, you’ll have to dive deeper into the Playtime Co. toy factory to find out what happened there. You’ll need to grapple and swing to safety, as well as solve puzzles to move forward. Just don’t let Mommy catch you. 

Other games coming to PS Plus soon

Those are a few of the games PlayStation Plus Premium and Extra subscribers can play in October. Here are the other games those subscribers can expect on Oct. 20, unless otherwise noted.

Dino Crisis 2*

The Midnight Walk: Available now.

Monster Energy Supercross 25: Available on Oct. 27.

Mycopunk

RollerCoaster Tycoon 3 Complete Edition*

Tales of Arise – Beyond the Dawn Edition: Available on Oct. 27.

* PlayStation Plus Premium subscription required.

title: Here’s how HomeView’s facial recognition works
snippet: Apple announced its HomeView smart display this morning. Apple says HomeView can recognize up to six different people to deliver a “personalized experience” for each user. John Gruber at Daring Fireball has more details on how HomeView’s facial recognition feature works. more…
fullText:
Apple announced its HomeView smart display this morning. Apple says HomeView can recognize up to six different people to deliver a “personalized experience” for each user.

John Gruber at Daring Fireball has more details on how HomeView’s facial recognition feature works.

HomeView’s face recognition support

According to Gruber, a user must have a “registered personal device” with Apple Intelligence support in order to be “recognized” by HomeView. That device must be on the home’s Wi-Fi network and have been “recently unlocked.”

Your first question might be how this facial recognition to identify users works, using a Center Stage camera alone, when other products (like, notably, the iPhone Duo) don’t let you unlock using the camera alone. HomeView does not have FaceID. I asked about this and Apple reps said that first, your home is (reasonably!) presumed to be a safe space. But in order for users to be recognized — by voice or face — they must have a “registered personal device” that supports Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, that device must be present on the home’s Wi-Fi network, and it must have been recently unlocked.

Gruber also points to a footnote from the HomeView press release, which reads:

Personal context requests require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad running the latest software version with Siri AI turned on and set to a supported language.

This means the Apple Watch does not count as a “registered personal device” for facial recognition on HomeView.

HomeView is available to pre-order today for $299 and will be released on November 13.

title: HomeView isn’t launching in the EU, here’s why
snippet: Apple unveiled its new HomeView product today, and it’s available for pre-order now. But unfortunately HomeView isn’t coming to the EU, at least for now. Here’s why. more…
fullText:
Apple unveiled its new HomeView product today, and it’s available for pre-order now. But unfortunately HomeView isn’t coming to the EU, at least for now. Here’s why.

Apple cites Siri AI’s absence from iOS as reason why it can’t launch HomeView in EU

Today Apple launched its Siri AI-centric ‘HomeView’ smart display product.

But if you’re in the EU, you can’t order one yet. And that’s not a mistake or oversight.

Per Apple’s press release:

Apple HomeView is not available for sale in the European Union, as Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS in the EU. Apple is working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward.

	

It’s a surprising decision, since presumably Apple could launch HomeView with Siri AI in the EU—just not with support for features that tie in with iOS 27.

Siri AI is available with macOS Golden Gate and visionOS 27 in the EU, for example. That’s because macOS and visionOS aren’t deemed gatekeeper platforms the way iOS is by the Digital Markets Act.

If Apple did launch HomeView in the EU, it would likely need to disable certain personal context features related to Siri AI. And it seems the company believes a compromised experience like that wouldn’t be worth it. So it’s holding out until Siri AI is able to come to iPhone users in the EU.

What do you make of Apple’s decision to not launch HomeView in the EU? Let us know in the comments.

title: Google Fitbit Edge hands-on: Pixel Watch Lite, take two
snippet: Google’s new Fitbit Edge tracker launches later this month and, as we get our review together, here’s a quick hands-on look at the new middle child of Google’s wearable lineup. more…
fullText:
Google’s new Fitbit Edge tracker launches later this month and, as we get our review together, here’s a quick hands-on look at the new middle child of Google’s wearable lineup.

The Fitbit Edge sits in between the screen-less Fitbit Air and the pricey & premium Pixel Watch 5. It’s the same slot that Google last addressed with the Fitbit Charge 6 back in 2023, but it does bring some changes this time around that make it even more of a “Pixel Watch Lite” than the Charge 6 already was.

As detailed in our launch coverage, the Fitbit Edge’s biggest upgrade over prior Fitbit trackers is the screen.

Google announces $179 Fitbit Edge tracker with display, GPS

It’s a much bigger canvas that fits a lot more on it, including new software tweaks that make it feel a lot more like a Pixel Watch than the Charge did. That includes both the faces and the different panels that Google has already shown. I’m thrilled to see a tactile power button on the side, too, as that was one of my biggest frustrations on the last Charge (even though Abner actually preferred it).

	

The hardware as a whole is simple, and we’ll get to how it feels to wear at a later date – we’re not allowed to share any in-depth insights or impressions from use on the Edge just yet, so this is really just a hands-on look.

Fitbit Edge is a fitness tracker first, supporting the usual heart rate, sleep, and workout tracking, as well as featuring the same live connection to both the Google Health app and third-party equipment for heart rate broadcasting and workout tracking. But it does more than that. With its display, it can also display notifications and calls from your phone, and it also has GPS that works with Google Maps.

I’m a bit disheartened to see that Google Wallet isn’t supported as it was on the Fitbit Charge 6, so that’s certainly a knock for the Fitbit Edge in my book. As for how that affects the overall experience, we’ll have to actually get into use to see more.

	

Continuing the Pixel Watch trend, Fitbit Edge uses the same style of Active Band, though with a connector that’s ripped from the Charge series. I was also pleasantly surprised to see that the Edge uses the exact same charger as the Air – I’m not sure who would use these two side-by-side, but it might be nice if you have a companion using the other tracker.

We’ll be digging into the Fitbit Edge over the coming weeks, so stay tuned!

Fitbit Edge officially launches on October 27, so you can probably take a guess when you’ll see our review. Pre-orders are open now.

title: Pocket Casts app now available on Android TV
snippet: After first coming to Apple TV, the official Pocket Casts app is now available to download on Android TV and Google TV devices. more…
fullText:
After first coming to Apple TV, the official Pocket Casts app is now available to download on Android TV and Google TV devices.

Officially teased when launching for Apple TV, it has taken a few months to be converted for Android set-top boxes. Unlike casting from your phone or tablet, this is a native app built from the ground up to work once paired with an existing account.

The dedicated experience is tailored to your TV, with a few refinements, including a dedicated “Made for TV” section for video podcasts with promoted content and highlighted content that you can watch and listen to simultaneously. It looks almost identical to the Apple TV version from what we can glean.

You pair using a QR code, and all of your podcast subscriptions, playlists, and account data will be synced with the application. You’re able to start a podcast playing and then close the application or minimize it, and it will continue playing. Any upcoming podcasts in your queue will appear as quick links, allowing you to switch quickly or pick up where you left off, as playback information across your devices is retained.

	

It’s worth noting that this has taken a couple of weeks to become widely available, as the app was noted in a recent changelog. You may have difficulty when searching directly on a Google TV or Android TV device, but you can “force” Pocket Casts to download from a browser by selecting any of your connected devices on the Play Store.

title: WhatsApp takes on Zoom and Google Meet with guest calling
snippet: WhatsApp users can now invite others to join group and one-on-one calls even if they don’t have an account. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
WhatsApp users can now invite others to join group and one-on-one calls even if they don’t have an account. Here are the details.

’Free, end-to-end encrypted calls for everyone with no time limits’

Today, WhatsApp announced the official rollout of guest calling, a feature that lets users “invite anyone to join a WhatsApp call – even if they don’t have a WhatsApp account.”

According to WhatsApp, guests must always be approved by the call host before joining, whether it’s a one-on-one call or a group call with up to 32 participants.

Guests enter a waiting room before being admitted, and hosts can remove them at any time. Guests also cannot see other participants’ phone numbers, send messages, or invite additional people.

WhatsApp says guest calling supports features such as screen sharing, hand-raising, and emoji-based reactions. Guests can also join directly from a computer browser, without installing the app.

Here’s WhatsApp on the new feature:

To get started, navigate to the Calls tab in WhatsApp, select the “+” icon, create a call link, and send it to the people you want to talk to – colleagues, classmates, or tutor – without having to worry about what apps they have.

Today’s launch comes after WhatsApp expanded testing of a similar feature for text conversations earlier this year, allowing users to exchange end-to-end encrypted messages with people who don’t have a WhatsApp account. At the time, however, the feature didn’t support voice or video calls.

Back to today’s news, WhatsApp also announced it is working on integrations with Google Calendar and Outlook, which will allow users to create WhatsApp call links directly from their calendars and add them to event invitations. The feature will require a WhatsApp plugin and is expected to launch later this year.

title: Apple’s two HomeViews have one big hidden difference
snippet: Today Apple unveiled HomeView, its long-awaited smart home hub. The HomeView comes in two distinct models, one with a domed speaker base and the other designed for wall mounting. But there’s a hidden feature difference beyond the form factors. more…
fullText:
Today Apple unveiled HomeView, its long-awaited smart home hub. The HomeView comes in two distinct models, one with a domed speaker base and the other designed for wall mounting. But there’s a hidden feature difference beyond the form factors.

HomeView speaker system is much more powerful on model with domed base

If you’re trying to decide which HomeView form factor to buy, there’s a key detail you should know about.

Beyond the obvious design differences between the model with a domed base—‘HomeView’—and the one designed for your wall—‘HomeView (Wall Mounted)’—there’s a disparity in capabilities too.

The standard HomeView has a much more powerful speaker system built in. Here are Apple’s descriptions of each speaker setup:

HomeView delivers room-filling sound with support for Spatial Audio, making it a great way to enjoy music and podcasts at home. Its custom-engineered acoustic system combines a down-firing woofer and two full-range drivers to produce deep bass and crisp highs. Powered by the A18 chip and built-in sensors, computational audio continuously optimizes the loudness and bass response at any volume. 

HomeView (Wall Mounted) brings full, balanced sound with two custom drivers and computational audio tuned specifically for on-wall placement, along with support for Spatial Audio.

	

Echoing this, Apple’s technical specs page confirms both models have two custom full-range drivers, but the HomeView with domed base adds:

Custom down-firing woofer

Dual force-cancelling passive radiators

Essentially, if you want the best sound experience from your HomeView, you’ll want to buy the standard model.

But if audio quality isn’t as important to you, the wall-mounted version will probably get the job done. It still has built-in speakers, but it won’t deliver the same performance and thus isn’t as well-suited for everyday music playback.

title: iPhone Duo Preorders Sell Out in Minutes: Backordered Until January
snippet: Demand is strong for Apple’s first foldable, which will first be available on Oct. 23.
fullText:
Apple’s iPhone Duo, its first foldable phone, is a hot ticket, judging by the preorders. 

Preorders for the iPhone Duo began on Friday at 5 a.m. PT, on Apple’s website and the Apple Store app. Although the phone has an Oct. 23 release date, as of now preordered models won’t ship until Jan. 29. If you want the phone sooner than 2027, you can try to buy one in stores on Oct. 23. 

		

			

CNET Senior Tech Reporter Abrar Al Heeti got to handle the iPhone Duo briefly ahead of preorders, and described it as essentially a compact iPhone that can double as an iPad Mini, well suited for consuming media. Beyond that, she wrote, “It has a satisfying feel and really makes the crease virtually disappear when the screen is on.”

The 7.6-inch screen when opened is the largest iPhone display screen yet (there’s also a 5.4-inch outer display). The Duo is also equipped with two 48-megapixel cameras: a main camera and an ultrawide one.  It’s geared for multitasking, with Apple Pencil support and drag-and-drop functionality similar to an iPad. 

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999, but trade-in offers and Apple’s Upgrade program could lower how much you pay out of pocket.

Apple is years late to the folding phone market, though that might not matter much to those already in the iPhone ecosystem. The bigger question is whether the iPhone Duo will be tempting to those inclined to buy Android phones, where the latest hinged options include the Samsung Galaxy Fold 8 and Galaxy Flip 8 and the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

title: M6 MacBook Pro: Three new upgrades launching later this month
snippet: Apple has a new M6 MacBook Pro launching later this month with a 14-inch screen and the current industrial design. And with its M6 chip, there are three upgrades we can expect from the new MacBook Pro. more…
fullText:
Apple has a new M6 MacBook Pro launching later this month with a 14-inch screen and the current industrial design. And with its M6 chip, there are three upgrades we can expect from the new MacBook Pro.

#1: Dual 16-core Neural Engine

If AI is in any way significant to your workflows—and with macOS 27’s AI features, it will be for more users—then the M6 MacBook Pro could be a big upgrade.

That’s because the M6 chip includes a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, up from the standard 16-core version available in M5 and prior. Per Apple:

M6 also introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, providing up to 2x the peak compute over previous generations to make on-device AI workflows run even faster. System frameworks can automatically utilize both engines simultaneously, enabling applications to see faster model execution.

#2: 12-core CPU and GPU with powerful new cores

The base M6 chip offers a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU. Both are solid upgrades over the M5, which was limited to 10 cores each.

M6’s CPU cores are especially interesting, as Apple is bringing three distinct core types to its base chip for the first time. It has 2 super cores, 4 performance cores, and 6 efficiency cores. Here’s what Apple says about each core:

Super cores: “blaze through single-threaded workloads”

Performance cores: “use less power and join the super cores to run demanding multithreaded workloads”

Efficiency cores: “handle everyday background tasks”

Previously only M5 Pro, M5 Max, and M5 Ultra provided super cores and performance cores in a single chip. But now these Pro-level capabilities are available for standard M6 users.

#3: Major efficiency gains to likely improve battery life

M6 is the first Apple chip built on a new 2nm process. And the company says that brings the benefit of “a major leap in performance and power efficiency.”

title: Google’s Fitbit Air is getting a shiny new Metal Mesh band and better automatic tracking
snippet: The Fitbit Air is finally getting another band option that isn’t fabric or polyurethane. Instead, the Metal Mesh band might actually take the Fitbit Air up a notch. more…
fullText:
The Fitbit Air is finally getting another band option that isn’t fabric or polyurethane. Instead, the Metal Mesh band might actually take the Fitbit Air up a notch.

Band selection for the Fitbit Air has been limited. The Elevated Modern band and Performance Loop options are good, but they lack a little flair. The Fitbit Air needed another band option to take advantage of just how easy it is to swap styles.

The Metal Mesh band fills that gap. It comes in Polished Silver and Champagne Gold with the intent of matching your existing jewelry. The look lets the wearable blend in with an elevated outfit, even if the Performance Loop band does a good job fitting most looks.

Google says the Metal Mesh band for the Fitbit Air will be priced at $69.99. You’ll also be able to buy the Fitbit Air with the Metal Mesh band and the Performance Loop band for $149.99 as a bundle, but it only comes in gold. That’s $20 more than the special editions, like the Steph Curry band and the Pokémon Sleep band, but it comes with two bands instead of a single option.

	

Packed into the band announcement, Google detailed a couple more feature additions to the Fitbit Air, regardless of band choice.

Google announced Health Guardian features that analyze your overall health picture. For Google Health Premium users who set up blood pressure and insulin resistance trends in the app, a report will be available each month to guide lifestyle adjustments. This may give the AI Health Coach some more usability for the average Fitbit user.

Google also notes that automatic activity tracking is getting an overhaul. According to the new post, Google claims the improvements will result in “more intelligent, accurate, and reliable” tracking.

Tracks more activities: We expanded the number of activities your Fitbit tracker or Pixel Watch can detect from 10 to more than 100, including strength training, swimming, and racket and team sports.

Uses more context: Powered by contextual reasoning, Google Health factors in critical context — including your workout routines, historical data, manual edits, and, with permission, your location — to deliver nearly 2x more accurate detections and cut missed workouts by more than half. 7

Logs workouts automatically: Workouts that meet your minimum duration threshold (15 minutes by default) with a sustained elevated heart rate are automatically logged, and a summary is sent to your mobile app, typically within 30 minutes.

Learns your patterns: When you confirm or edit an activity, you’re improving a feature that learns your unique patterns and uses them to refine its predictions.

These updates are planned for “later this month.” This comes as the company recently announced a more expensive $179 tracker called the Fitbit Edge. Unlike the Fitbit Air, this model has a screen carrying Google’s Material You design language.

As for the new Metal Mesh bands, Google has them available for pre-order on its website and at Target. It looks like the new bands should ship later this month.

title: If a Chromebook wasn’t for you, Googlebook isn’t either
snippet: Let’s not pretend; if you weren’t sold on a Chromebook, Googlebook isn’t for you either. more…
fullText:
Let’s not pretend; if you weren’t sold on a Chromebook, Googlebook isn’t for you either.

In our review of Googlebook as a platform, Abner Li explains how this platform sets a foundation for a potentially fascinating future. But, even from that viewpoint, it’s hard to ignore the shortcomings. Between the app gap and plenty of overlooked mistakes throughout the OS, Googlebook is far from a “finished” product.

In many ways, it continues to resemble what it’s replacing, ChromeOS, and that’s not going to leave the best impression for everyone.

Chromebook launched to a market starved of capable and reliable cheap laptops, and at a time where even higher-end machines were inherently compromised. Better battery life, no virus protection, simpler setup, price, take your pick, a Chromebook was a genuinely good choice for quite a while. But, as time went on, that math started to shift away from Google’s favor. I’d argue that it’s harder to find a bad laptop than it is a good one now, and there are good options on every price point, whether you’re looking at Windows or a MacBook. There’s an abundance of fully-capable Windows machines with long battery life and plenty of power, and frankly, the MacBook Air is $1,099.

	

With that in mind, Googlebook’s inherent similarities to ChromeOS betray any progress it might have made.

Under the hood, the new Android base is a much better foundation for the years to come. On the surface, where the users are, Googlebook hasn’t addressed any of the issues ChromeOS was dealing with, at least from a functional level. Apps are the biggest problem, as everything from mainstays to the niche library of apps are a shell on Googlebook of what they are on Windows and macOS. Unless you’re heavily using the web or Android apps for everything you do, you’re going to run into times where Googlebook is simply incapable of doing the things you want. And that even goes for Google’s own product offerings. Within the past week Google announced a new app that could combine voice recordings, shorthand notes, and local AI processing to build out detailed notes of a meeting or presentation. It’s a really useful and fun idea, but you literally cannot use it on Googlebook — it’s exclusive to Mac. 

Even the whole “this is a laptop for Android users” schtick doesn’t hold any water. These features are nonexistent at launch for most users, and ChromeOS had the vast majority of these anyway. 

	

Put simply, Googlebook isn’t a reset from ChromeOS. It’s not catching up to the competition. It’s the same old problems (plus a few new ones) in an admittedly much faster and more polished new chassis. The future might tell a different story but, at least for now, Googlebook is not for you if a Chromebook wasn’t.

title: Apple SVP Greg Joswiak: ‘We don’t feel threatened’ by OpenAI hardware plans
snippet: Today in a new story at TIME, the publication interviewed CEO John Ternus but also spoke to Greg “Joz” Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of Worldwide Marketing, who addressed the “lunatic fringe” of AI in Silicon Valley, hardware threats from OpenAI, and more. more…
fullText:
Today in a new story at TIME, the publication interviewed CEO John Ternus but also spoke to Greg “Joz” Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of Worldwide Marketing, who addressed the “lunatic fringe” of AI in Silicon Valley, hardware threats from OpenAI, and more.

Here’s what Greg Joswiak said about Apple’s AI strategy, threats from OpenAI, more

TIME picked the iPhone Duo as one of 2026’s best inventions and interviewed CEO John Ternus plus a few other Apple execs for the story.

One of those other interviewees, SVP of Worldwide Marketing Greg Joswiak, addressed Apple’s AI strategy, OpenAI hardware efforts, and more.

When asked about the ChatGPT maker’s hardware plans, Joswiak said: “We don’t feel threatened. The fact that we can do the integration that we can means we can create just a better experience than anybody else.” 

Apple’s integration of hardware, software, and services has long been central to the company’s product ethos. And it clearly believes those ecosystem strengths will be a strong defense against new competitors.

	

Joswiak also implies that perhaps OpenAI’s products won’t have as broad appeal as Apple devices do. From the story’s very next paragraph:

Joswiak adds that Apple isn’t making products for the die-hard AI believers chasing superintelligence. “We love them, and they can use it too, but that’s not our target,” he says. “It’s how to make it better for everyday people.”

This sort of split between the average person and the AI enthusiast is also highlighted by Joswiak elsewhere in the interview. Andrew Chow writes:

While Apple trains its own models, it is nowhere near the technology’s frontier, leaving the company vulnerable to being left behind if super-smart AI transforms industry and society in the coming years…But Ternus and other Apple executives say they aren’t concerned. In the midst of a populist AI backlash, they contend that they are building a modest but personalized and privacy-preserving form of AI that will actually help ordinary people as opposed to merely dazzling Silicon Valley’s “lunatic fringe,” as Greg Joswiak, senior vice president of worldwide marketing, puts it.

Joswiak doesn’t define this “lunatic fringe,” but by contrasting it with Apple’s own efforts to “help ordinary people,” he’s making a clear distinction.

title: John Ternus talks iPhone Duo, ‘cheap and crappy’ foldables in new interview
snippet: TIME has just published its list of the best inventions of 2026, and iPhone Duo made the list with John Ternus featured on the magazine cover. Here’s what Ternus said in his interview with TIME. more…
fullText:
TIME has just published its list of the best inventions of 2026, and iPhone Duo made the list with John Ternus featured on the magazine cover. Here’s what Ternus said in his interview with TIME.

John Ternus on iPhone Duo origins, delay to market, more

John Ternus sat down with TIME for a wide-ranging interview centered on iPhone Duo, but also covering a variety of other topics, including AI.

Regarding the iPhone Duo, which is hitting the market nearly a decade after other foldables, Ternus was involved in early foldable work at Apple all the way back in 2011.

In 2011, when many people still carried around flip phones, Ternus and five other engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, exploring what kind of batteries and circuit boards might be needed for such an idea. “It felt clear that we were going to eventually get to a place where OLED displays were going to be flexible,” Ternus says.

Ternus wasn’t a fan of early attempts at foldables from other companies in the 2010s. He says, “The other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy.”

The drive to achieve a foldable unlike its competitors is evidenced by a story from Richard Dinh, Apple’s VP of Product Design.

Along the way, Ternus encouraged the team to invest more time and effort in the project, even as other foldables beat them to market. Dinh says that at one point, he asked Ternus whether his team should proceed with a top surface material similar to those of its competitors, which Dinh felt had flaws but was potentially good enough.

“And he was like, ‘Look, Rich, you’ll know when it’s the right thing.’ And that gave us the confidence to really push the boundaries on innovation and manufacturing, and fly worldwide to connect our suppliers together and come up with the nanotexture [a surface technology],” Dinh says. The result—a surface made from a custom polymer and built atop a hinge with more than 100 tiny interior precision components—has impressed its first users, who have said they can barely detect a crease at all.

	

The story also mentions that Ternus “has devoted much of his early tenure as CEO to obsessing over design, spending multiple days a week in the studio with the industrial-design and human-interface teams.” This echoes previous Bloomberg reporting around Ternus’s early priorities.

Other topics Ternus addresses in the interview include:

Apple Intelligence’s reliance on Gemini technology: “There’s not really a goal that we have to make every single thing in a product. We make the things where we can really bring differentiation.”

Siri AI’s unique advantages: “Everything in your life is on your phone. With Siri AI, you can leverage all that information to do things, learn things, and figure out things in a way that nobody else can do.”

Not sleeping much before September event: “I was on such a moment of adrenaline and caffeine and excitement for the day.”
